heading: What is Adderall?
text: Adderall (mixed amphetamine and dextroamphetamine salts) is a central nervous system stimulant used to treat attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and a sleep disorder called narcolepsy. Adderall contains a combination of amphetamine and dextroamphetamine, which affect chemicals in the brain and nerves that contribute to hyperactivity and impulse control. For ADHD, Adderall is used in children 3 to 17 years of age and in adults. It may help increase attention and decrease impulsiveness and hyperactivity. For narcolepsy, Adderall is used in people 6 years and older. It is not known if Adderall is safe and effective for ADHD in children under 3 years of age or for narcolepsy in children under 6 years of age. Adderall is a federally controlled substance (CII) because it contains amphetamine, which can be a target for people who abuse prescription medicines or street drugs. Keep Adderall in a safe place to protect it from theft. Never give your Adderall to anyone else, because it may cause death or harm them. Selling or giving away Adderall is against the law. Adderall may also be used for purposes not listed in this medication guide. Adderall (mixed amphetamine and dextroamphetamine salts) was FDA-approved on January 19, 1960. Extended-release formulations of Adderall (Adderall XR) are only used to treat ADHD.

heading: Warnings
text: Adderall has a Boxed Warning for abuse, misuse, and addiction. Abuse, misuse, and addiction: Adderall has a high chance of abuse and misuse and may lead to substance use problems, including addiction. Misuse and abuse of Adderall, other amphetamine-containing medicines, and methylphenidate-containing medicines can lead to overdose and death. The risk of overdose and death is increased with higher doses or when the medicine is used in ways that are not approved, such as snorting or injection. Adderall may lead to physical dependence after prolonged use, even if taken as directed. Your healthcare provider should check you or your child for the risk of abuse, misuse, and addiction before starting treatment and will monitor you or your child during treatment. Tell your healthcare provider if you or your child has ever abused or been dependent on alcohol, prescription medicines, or street drugs. Heart-related risks: Stimulants have caused stroke, heart attack, and sudden death in people with high blood pressure, heart disease, or a heart defect. Your healthcare provider should check you or your child carefully for heart problems before starting Adderall and should check blood pressure and heart rate regularly during treatment. Call your healthcare provider right away or go to the nearest hospital emergency room if you or your child have any signs of heart problems, such as chest pain, shortness of breath, or fainting during treatment. heading: Warnings
text: Adderall may cause new or worse behavior and thought problems, new or worse bipolar illness, or new psychotic symptoms (such as hearing voices, or seeing or believing things that are not real) or new manic symptoms. This is more likely if you have a history of depression, mental illness, or bipolar disorder. Tell your healthcare provider about any mental problems you or your child have, or about a family history of suicide, bipolar illness, or depression. Call your healthcare provider right away if you or your child have any new or worsening mental symptoms during treatment, especially hearing voices, seeing or believing things that are not real, or new manic symptoms. Circulation problems: You may have blood circulation problems that can cause numbness, pain, or discoloration in your fingers or toes. Call your doctor right away if you have unexplained wounds appearing on your fingers or toes during treatment. Other warnings: Do not use Adderall if you have used an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days, such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, or tranylcypromine, or if you have received a methylene blue injection. A dangerous drug interaction could occur. You may not be able to use Adderall if you have glaucoma, an overactive thyroid, severe anxiety or agitation, moderate to severe high blood pressure, heart disease or coronary artery disease, vascular disease, or a history of drug or alcohol addiction.

heading: How should I take Adderall?
text: Take Adderall exactly as prescribed by your healthcare provider. Follow all directions on your prescription label. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose. Do not take this medicine in larger or smaller amounts or for longer than recommended. The first dose of the day is usually taken when you first wake up. Taking this medicine in the afternoon may cause trouble sleeping. Adderall can be taken with or without food. Do not crush or chew an extended-release capsule. Swallow it whole. To make swallowing easier, you may open the capsule and sprinkle the medicine into a spoonful of applesauce, then swallow all of the mixture right away without chewing. Do not divide the medicine in the capsule, and do not save the mixture for later use. Adderall may be habit-forming. Never share this medicine with another person, especially someone with a history of drug abuse or addiction. Keep the medicine where others cannot get to it. While using this medicine, your doctor will need to check your progress at regular visits. Adderall can cause unusual results with certain medical tests, so tell any doctor who treats you that you are using this medicine. Your healthcare provider may tell you to stop taking this medicine for a short time before you get certain imaging tests.

heading: What happens if I overdose?
text: If you or your child takes too much Adderall, call your healthcare provider or the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222, or go to the nearest hospital emergency room right away. An overdose of Adderall could be fatal. Overdose symptoms may include restlessness, tremor, muscle twitches, rapid breathing, confusion, hallucinations, panic, aggressiveness, muscle pain or weakness, and dark colored urine. These symptoms may be followed by depression and tiredness. Other symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, uneven heartbeats, feeling light-headed, fainting, seizure, or coma.

heading: What to avoid
text: This medicine may impair your thinking or reactions. Be careful if you drive or do anything that requires you to be alert. Avoid drinking fruit juices or taking vitamin C at the same time you take Adderall. These can make your body absorb less of the medicine.

heading: What other drugs will affect Adderall?
text: Ask your doctor before using a stomach acid medicine (including Alka-Seltzer or sodium bicarbonate). Some of these medicines can change the way your body absorbs Adderall and may increase side effects. Some medicines can interact with amphetamine and dextroamphetamine and cause a serious condition called serotonin syndrome. Tell your doctor about all your current medicines and any you start or stop using, especially: selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) tricyclic antidepressants medicines used to treat migraine headaches, called triptans lithium, buspirone, tramadol, fentanyl, or tryptophan St. John's Wort blood pressure medicine heartburn medicine a blood thinner such as warfarin cold or allergy medicine that contains a decongestant opioid (narcotic) medicine seizure medicine. This list is not complete, and many other drugs can interact with Adderall, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Give a list of all your medicines to any healthcare provider who treats you. Do not start any new medicine during treatment with Adderall without talking to your healthcare provider first.

heading: How should I store and dispose of Adderall?
text: Store Adderall at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Protect Adderall from light. Store Adderall in a safe place, such as a locked cabinet, and keep it out of the reach of children. Dispose of remaining, unused, or expired Adderall through a medicine take-back program at a US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) authorized collection site. If no take-back program or DEA-authorized collector is available, mix Adderall with an undesirable, nontoxic substance such as dirt, cat litter, or used coffee grounds to make it less appealing to children and pets. Place the mixture in a sealed container such as a plastic bag and throw it away in the household trash. Visit www.fda.gov/drugdisposal for more information on disposing of unused medicines.

Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) is a prodrug that converts into dexamphetamine once absorbed by the body. text: Q: Modafinil (Provigil) vs Adderall: What's the difference? A: Modafinil and Adderall are both classified as CNS stimulants but have different chemical structures, which means there are differences in their addiction potential and risk of side effects. text: Q: How do you get rid of Adderall tongue? A: Adderall tongue is a common side effect of Adderall that can detrimentally and seriously affect a person’s quality of life. heading: What is albuterol inhalation?
text: Albuterol is a bronchodilator that relaxes muscles in the airways and increases air flow to the lungs. Albuterol inhalation is used to treat or prevent bronchospasm, or narrowing of the airways in the lungs, in people with asthma or certain types of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). It is also used to prevent exercise-induced bronchospasm. Albuterol inhalation is for use in adults and children who are at least 2 years old. Always follow your doctor's directions when giving albuterol to a child.

heading: Warnings
text: It is important to keep albuterol on hand at all times. Get your prescription refilled before you run out of medicine completely. Keep using all of your other medications as prescribed by your doctor. Talk with your doctor if any of your asthma medications do not seem to work as well in treating or preventing attacks. If it seems like you need to use more of any of your medications in a 24-hour period, talk with your doctor. An increased need for medication could be an early sign of a serious asthma attack. Only use albuterol as prescribed by your physician. An overdose of albuterol can be fatal. Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.

heading: What is allopurinol?
text: Allopurinol belongs to a class of medications called xanthine oxidase inhibitors. It works by reducing the production of uric acid in the body. High levels of uric acid may cause gout attacks or kidney stones. Allopurinol is used to treat gout (a type of arthritis in which uric acid, a naturally occurring substance in the body, builds up in the joints and causes sudden attacks of redness, swelling, pain, and heat in one or more joints). Allopurinol is used to prevent gout attacks, not to treat them once they occur. Allopurinol does not need to be stopped during an acute flare. Allopurinol is also used to treat high levels of uric acid that builds up in the blood as tumors break down in people with certain types of cancer who are being treated with chemotherapy medications. It is also used to treat kidney stones that have come back in people who have high levels of uric acid in their urine.

heading: Warnings
text: You should not use this medicine if you have ever had an allergic reaction to allopurinol. Allopurinol can lower blood cells that help your body fight infections. This can make it easier for you to bleed from an injury or get sick from being around others who are ill. Your blood may need to be tested often. Visit your doctor regularly. In rare cases, allopurinol may cause a severe allergic reaction. Stop taking this medicine and call your doctor right away if you have painful urination, blood in your urine, burning in your eyes, swelling in your face or throat, skin redness or a rash that spreads and causes blistering and peeling. Avoid drinking alcohol. It can make your condition worse. Allopurinol may impair your thinking or reactions. Be careful if you drive or do anything that requires you to be alert.

heading: What is cyclobenzaprine?
text: Cyclobenzaprine is a prescription muscle relaxant used short-term to relieve muscle spasms caused by sprains, strains, and injuries, including low back and neck pain. It is used together with rest and physical therapy to help relieve the pain, tenderness, and limited movement caused by muscle spasm. 1,2 Cyclobenzaprine is also used to treat fibromyalgia in adults, where it can help reduce pain. For fibromyalgia, it is taken as a sublingual (under the tongue) tablet at bedtime under the brand name Tonmya. In clinical trials, Tonmya significantly reduced fibromyalgia pain compared with placebo over 14 weeks, and close to half of treated patients achieved at least a 30% improvement in pain. 3 The Flexeril brand has been discontinued, but cyclobenzaprine is available as generic tablets and as the brand-name products Amrix (extended-release capsules) and Fexmid. 2,4

heading: How does cyclobenzaprine work?
text: Cyclobenzaprine works by reducing the nerve signals in the brain that drive muscle tone and spasm, which allows tight, overactive muscles to relax. It acts within the central nervous system, primarily at the level of the brain stem, and does not act on the muscles themselves or at the junction between nerves and muscle. 1,2 Because cyclobenzaprine works through the nervous system in this way, it will not relieve muscle spasm caused by central nervous system disease, such as cerebral palsy or spinal cord disease. 1,2 The way cyclobenzaprine works in fibromyalgia is not known. Laboratory studies show it blocks several receptor types, including serotonin (5-HT2A), histamine, and muscarinic receptors. 3 Cyclobenzaprine is chemically related to tricyclic antidepressants such as amitriptyline, which explains several of its side effects (such as drowsiness and dry mouth) and some of its most important drug interactions. 1,2

heading: Is cyclobenzaprine a controlled substance or narcotic?
text: No. Cyclobenzaprine is not a controlled substance and is not a narcotic, opioid, or benzodiazepine. It is a skeletal muscle relaxant that is chemically related to tricyclic antidepressants, and its FDA labeling states directly that cyclobenzaprine is not a controlled substance. 3 Cyclobenzaprine is not considered addictive in the way opioids or benzodiazepines are. Stopping suddenly after prolonged use may rarely cause nausea, headache, and a general unwell feeling, but these effects are not a sign of addiction. 1,3

heading: What is duloxetine?
text: Duloxetine is a selective serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor antidepressant (SSNRI). Duloxetine affects chemicals in the brain that may be unbalanced in people with depression. heading: What is Fluoxetine?
text: Fluoxetine is a prescription antidepressant used to treat major depressive disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), bulimia nervosa, and panic disorder. When used together with olanzapine (Zyprexa), it is also used to treat depressive episodes associated with bipolar I disorder and treatment-resistant depression. Fluoxetine belongs to a class of antidepressants called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). The original brand name of fluoxetine is Prozac, and it's now available as a generic.

heading: What Is Fluoxetine Used For?
text: Fluoxetine is FDA-approved to treat the following conditions: Major depressive disorder (MDD) for acute and maintenance treatment in adults and children aged 8 years and older Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) for acute and maintenance treatment in adults and children aged 7 years and older Bulimia nervosa for acute and maintenance treatment of binge-eating and purging in adults with moderate to severe bulimia Panic disorder for the treatment of panic attacks in adults When used in combination with olanzapine, fluoxetine is also FDA-approved for: Acute treatment of depressive episodes associated with Bipolar I disorder (depressive episodes) in adults and children aged 10 years and older Treatment-resistant depression for adults who have not responded to at least two adequate antidepressant trials Fluoxetine alone is not approved for bipolar I depressive episodes or treatment-resistant depression - olanzapine must be used in combination for these indications.

heading: How does fluoxetine (Prozac) work?
text: Fluoxetine works by blocking the reabsorption (reuptake) of serotonin in the brain, leaving more of it active between nerve cells. Serotonin is a neurotransmitter that helps regulate mood, emotions, and sleep. By increasing the availability of serotonin, fluoxetine can relieve symptoms of depression, anxiety, and OCD. Fluoxetine belongs to a class of antidepressants called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). SSRIs are one of the most commonly prescribed antidepressant classes because they are generally well-tolerated and effective across a range of conditions. Most people need to take fluoxetine for 4 to 6 weeks before feeling the full effects.

heading: How does gabapentin work?
text: Gabapentin works by calming overactive electrical signals in the brain and nervous system. It does this by binding to the alpha-2-delta subunit of calcium channels in nerve cells, which is thought to normalize chemical signals nerves send to each other and results in a calmer, less excitable nerve circuit. That same effect helps in different ways depending on what gabapentin is treating: Epilepsy - dampens the runaway electrical firing that causes seizures. Postherpetic neuralgia (shingles nerve pain) - reduces the abnormal pain signals from nerves damaged by shingles. Restless legs syndrome (gabapentin enacarbil / Horizant) - the exact mechanism is less clear, but the same calming effect on overactive nerves is thought to ease the urge-to-move sensation. Gabapentin is not an opioid, sedative, or anti-inflammatory painkiller. It works directly on the nerves, which is why it helps nerve-related pain and why it isn't useful for everyday pain like headaches or sprains. Most people need 1 to 2 weeks of regular dosing for the full effect to build up.

text: Avoid driving or hazardous activities until you know how gabapentin will affect you. Dizziness or drowsiness can cause falls, accidents, or severe injuries. Avoid taking antacids at the same time as gabapentin. Do not drink alcohol. Dangerous side effects could occur.

heading: What other drugs will affect gabapentin?
text: Taking gabapentin with other medicines that make you drowsy or slow your breathing can cause dangerous side effects, including life-threatening breathing problems. Ask your doctor before using gabapentin with: opioid pain medicines such as hydrocodone, oxycodone, morphine, or buprenorphine sleeping pills such as zolpidem anxiety medicines such as lorazepam and other benzodiazepines muscle relaxers, sedatives, or other seizure medicines that cause drowsiness Avoid drinking alcohol while taking gabapentin, because it can add to these effects. Some medicines change the amount of gabapentin in your body: Antacids that contain aluminum or magnesium (such as Maalox) can reduce gabapentin absorption. Take gabapentin at least 2 hours after an antacid. Morphine can increase gabapentin levels, which may increase drowsiness and the risk of breathing problems. Your doctor may adjust your dose. Gabapentin does not usually interact with other seizure medicines, such as phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproic acid, or phenobarbital, because it is not broken down by the liver. Your doctor can still check for interactions with your specific medicines. Tell your doctor about all your current medicines, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. This list does not include all possible drug interactions.

heading: Popular FAQ
text: Q: Gabapentin for dogs: uses, dosage and side effects A: Gabapentin is commonly prescribed by veterinarians to treat dogs with chronic pain (such as arthritis, back pain, or nerve pain) or to relieve fear or anxiety associated with stressful events (such as car or plane travel, situations with loud noises [such as fireworks], or visits to the vets or the groomers). Q: Lyrica vs Gabapentin: What's the difference? A: Both Lyrica (pregabalin) and gabapentin (Neurontin) are both anticonvulsants and gabapentinoids used to treat nerve pain and seizures, but they differ significantly in potency, absorption speed, and regulatory status. Lyrica is generally more potent, faster-acting (peaks in approximately 1 hour), and is a Schedule V controlled substance, whereas gabapentin peaks in 3 to 4 hours, is less regulated in most states, and is usually cheaper. Q: How long does gabapentin withdrawal last? A: Case reports have shown that gabapentin withdrawal often lasts for 5 to 10 days, but some people have taken as long as 18 weeks to completely taper off gabapentin while managing withdrawal symptoms. The symptoms and how long they last depend on how much of the drug you are taking and for how long you’ve been taking it.

heading: Popular FAQ
text: Q: Is gabapentin considered a painkiller? A: Gabapentin (Neurontin, Gralise, Horizant) is commonly used to treat some types of nerve pain but is classified as an anticonvulsant medicine, not as an opioid or narcotic painkiller. Gabapentin is used to treat nerve pain that can occur due to an outbreak of shingles, restless legs syndrome (RLS), and some forms of epilepsy. Q: Is gabapentin safe for cats? A: Yes, Gabapentin is safe for cats when prescribed by a veterinarian. This medication is commonly used to treat cat pain, anxiety, and feline hyperesthesia syndrome with minimal side effects. Mild sedation and drowsiness are the most common reactions, which typically improve with continued use. Q: Does gabapentin help treat nerve pain? A: Gabapentin can help relieve nerve pain in some people with postherpetic neuralgia (shingles nerve pain) and diabetic peripheral neuropathy (diabetic foot pain). Q: How long does it take gabapentin to work? A: It can take several weeks for gabapentin to reach its full effect, but this depends on the condition being treated and your individual response to the drug. Q: Does gabapentin cause weight gain? A: Gabapentin may cause weight gain, but it is an uncommon side effect. Studies have shown that a small number of people taking gabapentin weight gain. People who do gain weight may gain about 5 pounds after 6 weeks of use.

heading: Popular FAQ
text: Q: Does gabapentin help you sleep? A: Gabapentin is a prescription medication that may help you sleep. That may be why it has been prescribed for people with insomnia, even though it is not approved for that use.

heading: What is hydrochlorothiazide?
text: Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic, often called a water pill, used to treat high blood pressure and to reduce a build-up of fluid in the body (edema). It works by making the kidneys pass more salt and water out of the body, so you urinate more. Hydrochlorothiazide is often shortened to HCTZ on prescriptions and medical records. It is available as a tablet, capsule, and liquid (suspension) taken by mouth and is usually taken once or twice a day. Hydrochlorothiazide is available as: oral tablet (12.5 mg, 25 mg, and 50 mg) oral capsule (12.5 mg) powder for oral suspension (10 mg/mL) Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) brand names included HydroDIURIL tablets (discontinued), Esidrix (discontinued), and Microzide capsules (discontinued); now generic tablets and capsules are available. The brand name of hydrochlorothiazide oral suspension is Inzirqo. Hydrochlorothiazide is also an ingredient in many combination blood pressure medicines, including with losartan, lisinopril, valsartan, and more.

heading: What is hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) used for?
text: Hydrochlorothiazide is approved to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and fluid retention (edema) in certain patients. High blood pressure: HCTZ is used to manage high blood pressure (hypertension), either on its own or alongside other blood pressure medicines. Lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events, mainly strokes and heart attacks. All three forms of hydrochlorothiazide, tablets, capsules and the oral suspension, are approved for high blood pressure in adults, and the oral suspension is also approved for children. Fluid retention: Hydrochlorothiazide tablets are used to treat a build-up of fluid (edema) associated with: congestive heart failure cirrhosis of the liver kidney conditions, including nephrotic syndrome, acute glomerulonephritis and chronic kidney failure treatment with corticosteroid or estrogen medicines The HCTZ oral suspension is approved for fluid retention associated with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis of the liver, and kidney disease including nephrotic syndrome, in both adults and children. The capsules are approved for high blood pressure only, not for fluid retention. Not all forms of HCTZ are approved for all indications and age groups. Approved HCTZ uses by age groups and dosage form: HCTZ Form and strengths | High blood pressure | Fluid retention (edema) | Ages

heading: What is hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) used for?
text: Tablets 12.5 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg | Yes | As an add-on therapy for edema due to congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, and corticosteroid and estrogen therapy. Yes, for edema due to various forms of renal dysfunction such as nephrotic syndrome, acute glomerulonephritis, and chronic renal failure. | Adults and children Capsules 12.5 mg | Yes | No | Adults Oral suspension 10 mg/mL | Yes | Yes, for edema due to congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, and renal disease including the nephrotic syndrome in adult and pediatric patients. | Adults and children

heading: How does hydrochlorothiazide work?
text: Hydrochlorothiazide works by inhibiting the kidneys from reabsorbing sodium and chloride, so more salt and water leave the body in the urine, which helps reduce excess fluid buildup (edema). Exactly how thiazides lower blood pressure is not fully understood. The early effect is thought to come from a drop in blood volume. With longer-term use, blood volume returns towards normal while the blood vessels themselves offer less resistance to blood flow. Hydrochlorothiazide does not usually change blood pressure that is already normal. Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic.

heading: Before taking this medicine
text: Do not take hydrochlorothiazide if you are unable to pass urine (anuria), or if you are allergic to hydrochlorothiazide or to other sulfonamide-derived medicines (sometimes called sulfa drugs). Before you start HCTZ, tell your doctor if you have or have ever had: kidney disease or reduced kidney function liver disease, including cirrhosis diabetes gout or high uric acid levels high cholesterol or high triglycerides high calcium levels or a parathyroid gland disorder low potassium or low sodium levels lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus) glaucoma an allergy to sulfa medicines or to penicillin Also tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Hydrochlorothiazide may cause jaundice or bleeding problems in a newborn. It can also pass into breast milk and may cause serious side effects in a nursing baby, so you and your doctor should decide whether you will take this medicine or breastfeed.

heading: Warning and precautions
text: Fluid and salt imbalance: Hydrochlorothiazide can lower the levels of potassium, sodium, magnesium and chloride in your blood. Low potassium (hypokalemia) is the most common of these and is more likely at higher doses, during rapid fluid loss, if you have severe cirrhosis, or after long-term use.. Your doctor will check your blood before you start and at intervals during treatment. Contact your doctor if you have any of the following, which can be signs of a fluid or salt imbalance: dry mouth, thirst, or unusual weakness or tiredness drowsiness, restlessness or confusion muscle pain, cramps or muscle fatigue fast heartbeat passing much less urine than usual nausea or vomiting seizures Kidney and liver problems: HCTZ reduces the fluid volume in your body, which can lead to sudden kidney injury. The risk is higher if you have chronic kidney disease, heart failure, or are already low on fluid. If you have liver disease, small changes in fluid and salt balance can trigger a serious complication called hepatic coma. Your doctor will monitor your kidney function and watch for changes in alertness. Sudden vision changes need urgent care:

heading: Warning and precautions
text: Rarely, hydrochlorothiazide causes sudden short-sightedness (acute myopia) and a sharp rise in pressure inside the eye (acute angle-closure glaucoma), usually within hours to weeks of starting the medicine. Stop taking it and get medical help immediately if your vision drops suddenly or your eye hurts. Left untreated, this can cause permanent loss of vision. A history of allergy to sulfa medicines or penicillin may increase the risk. Blood sugar, cholesterol, uric acid and calcium: Hydrochlorothiazide can raise blood sugar, cholesterol, triglycerides, uric acid and calcium. Your diabetes medicine or insulin dose may need adjusting, and diabetes that was previously unnoticed can become apparent during treatment. The rise in uric acid is related to the dose and can cause gout or make existing gout worse. Because the medicine also affects calcium, it is stopped before parathyroid function tests, so tell any doctor arranging tests that you take it. Your doctor will check these levels from time to time. Skin cancer risk: Long-term use of hydrochlorothiazide is linked to a small increase in the risk of non-melanoma skin cancer, mainly squamous cell carcinoma. In a large safety study the increase was about 1 extra case per 16,000 people per year, rising to about 1 extra case per 6,700 people per year among white patients who had taken a total of 50,000 mg or more.

heading: Warning and precautions
text: Protect your skin from the sun, wear protective clothing and use sunscreen, avoid sunlamps and tanning beds, and have regular skin checks. Tell your doctor about any new or changing skin growth, or a sore that does not heal. Lupus and allergic reactions: Thiazide diuretics have been reported to worsen lupus or bring it on. Sensitivity reactions can happen whether or not you have a history of allergies or asthma.

heading: Hydrochlorothiazide side effects
text: The most noticeable effect of hydrochlorothiazide is passing urine more often, particularly in the first few weeks. This is how the medicine works rather than a side effect, and it usually settles as your body adjusts. Serious side effects: Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction, such as hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat. Get emergency medical help if you have a severe skin reaction, such as a spreading red or purple rash with blistering and peeling, or skin that is painful to touch. Stop taking hydrochlorothiazide and get medical help immediately if you have a sudden change in your vision or pain in your eye. Call your doctor at once if you have: severe pain in your upper stomach that spreads to your back, with nausea and vomiting, which can be a sign of inflammation of the pancreas (pancreatitis) yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes (jaundice) fever, chills, sore throat, mouth sores or other signs of infection unusual bruising or bleeding, or pale skin and unusual tiredness, which can be signs of a blood problem shortness of breath, wheezing, or a cough with frothy mucus passing much less urine than usual, or swelling in your legs and ankles light-headedness or fainting, especially when standing up signs of dehydration or a salt imbalance, such as extreme thirst, dry mouth, confusion, muscle cramps, irregular heartbeat or unusual weakness Other side effects: Other hydrochlorothiazide side effects include:

heading: Hydrochlorothiazide side effects
text: dizziness, a spinning sensation (vertigo), headache, restlessness, or tingling and numbness (paresthesia) weakness nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, stomach cramping, stomach irritation, or loss of appetite muscle spasm increased sensitivity to sunlight, causing sunburn more easily hair loss or thinning difficulty getting or keeping an erection temporary blurred vision, or objects looking yellow-tinged (xanthopsia) swelling and tenderness of the salivary glands raised blood sugar, sugar in the urine, or raised uric acid If a side effect is moderate or severe, your doctor may lower your dose or stop the medicine. Do not stop taking HCTZ on your own without speaking to your doctor first. This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

heading: Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) dosage information
text: Your doctor will choose the smallest dose that controls your condition, and may adjust it over time. Follow your prescription label and do not change your dose yourself. HCTZ dose for high blood pressure (adults): Tablets: The starting dose is hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg once a day, which may be increased to 50 mg a day, taken as a single dose or split into two doses. Doses above 50 mg a day are often associated with a marked drop in blood potassium. Most people do not need more than 50 mg a day when hydrochlorothiazide is taken alongside other blood pressure medicines Capsules: The starting dose is a hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg capsule once a day, whether taken on its own or with other blood pressure medicines. Total daily doses above 50 mg are not recommended. Capsules are approved for high blood pressure only, not for fluid retention. HCTZ dose for fluid retention (adults): Tablets: The usual dose is hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg to 100 mg a day, taken as a single dose or split into two doses. Many people with fluid retention respond to intermittent treatment, such as taking it every other day or on 3 to 5 days each week. Excessive response and undesirable electrolyte imbalance are less likely to occur with intermittent dosing. HCTZ dose for children for high blood pressure and fluid retention:

heading: Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) dosage information
text: The usual HCTZ dose in children, for both high blood pressure and fluid retention, is 1 mg to 2 mg per kilogram of body weight (0.5 mg to 1 mg per pound) a day, given as a single dose or split into two doses. Infants under 6 months: may be need doses of up to 3 mg per kilogram (1.5 mg per pound) a day, given as two divided doses up to the same maximum 37.5 mg daily limit Infants and children under 2 years: do not exceed 37.5 mg a day Children 2 to 12 years: do not exceed 100 mg a day The dose is based on your child's weight and must be worked out by their doctor. Taking the oral suspension: If your child has been prescribed the liquid form (oral suspension), the following applies: Shake the bottle well before every dose. Measure each dose with the oral dosing syringe. Ask your pharmacist for a syringe and a bottle adapter if you do not have them. Never measure a dose with a household teaspoon or tablespoon, because these do not give an accurate amount. Store the made-up suspension at room temperature and do not freeze it. Throw away any unused suspension 30 days after it was made up. The pharmacist will write this date on the bottle. The oral suspension can be taken with or without food. What happens if I miss a dose?:

heading: Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) dosage information
text: Take the medicine as soon as you can, but skip the missed dose if it is almost time for your next dose. Do not take two doses at one time. What happens if I overdose?: Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. Overdose symptoms may include nausea, dizziness, dry mouth, thirst, and muscle pain or weakness.

heading: How long does hydrochlorothiazide take to work?
text: Hydrochlorothiazide starts to work within 2 hours of a dose, with the peak effect at about 4 hours. The increase in urine output lasts for around 6 to 12 hours, while the medicine's overall action on the body can persist for up to 24 hours. Lowering blood pressure takes longer than the fluid effect, and your doctor will usually reassess your blood pressure after a few weeks rather than straight away. The medicine is well absorbed, is not broken down by the body, and is cleared by the kidneys, with most of a dose passing out unchanged in the urine. Its half-life, meaning the time for blood levels to fall by half, has been reported as 6 to 15 hours. In people with kidney disease, levels in the blood are higher and the medicine stays in the body longer. Hydrochlorothiazide controls high blood pressure but does not cure it. Keep taking it even if you feel well, because high blood pressure often causes no symptoms.

heading: What other drugs will affect hydrochlorothiazide?
text: Tell your doctor and pharmacist about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Medicines that need particular care: Lithium. Lithium and diuretics generally should not be taken together. Hydrochlorothiazide reduces how quickly the kidneys clear lithium, which carries a high risk of lithium toxicity. Cholestyramine and colestipol. These cholesterol-lowering resins bind hydrochlorothiazide in the gut and can reduce how much you absorb by up to 85 percent for cholestyramine and 43 percent for colestipol. The doses need to be separated. For the oral suspension, the label advises taking hydrochlorothiazide at least 4 hours before, or 4 to 6 hours after, the resin. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), diclofenac, meloxicam, indomethacin, celecoxib and aspirin. These can reduce the fluid-clearing and blood-pressure-lowering effects of hydrochlorothiazide, and your doctor will check whether the medicine is still working as intended. Insulin and oral diabetes medicines. Your diabetes medicine dose may need adjusting. Corticosteroids and ACTH. Taken with hydrochlorothiazide, these increase the loss of salts from the body, particularly potassium. Digoxin and other digitalis medicines. Low potassium caused by hydrochlorothiazide can make the heart more sensitive to the toxic effects of digitalis, including irregular heart rhythms. Other blood pressure medicines. The effects add together, which may be intended, but can also lower blood pressure more than expected. Alcohol, barbiturates and opioid pain medicines. These can make the drop in blood pressure on standing worse, causing dizziness or fainting.

accepted.RefersTo: Alcohol, barbiturates and opioid pain medicines

heading: What other drugs will affect hydrochlorothiazide?
text: Muscle relaxants used during surgery (nondepolarizing muscle relaxants such as tubocurarine). You may respond more strongly to them, so tell your surgeon and anesthetist that you take hydrochlorothiazide. Medicines that raise blood pressure (pressor amines such as norepinephrine). Your response to them may be reduced, although this does not usually prevent their use. This list is not complete. Other medicines may affect hydrochlorothiazide, and hydrochlorothiazide may affect other medicines.

heading: Hydrochlorothiazide FAQ
text: Does hydrochlorothiazide cause weight loss?: Hydrochlorothiazide is not a weight loss medicine. Some people see the number on the scales drop in the first days or weeks of treatment, but this is extra fluid leaving the body rather than any loss of body fat, and it levels off. Do not take hydrochlorothiazide to lose weight. Can you drink alcohol while taking hydrochlorothiazide?: Alcohol can make the drop in blood pressure that happens when you stand up worse, which may leave you feeling dizzy or faint. The same applies to barbiturates and opioid pain medicines. Tell your doctor how much you drink so they can advise you. Does hydrochlorothiazide lower your potassium?: Yes. Hydrochlorothiazide can lower blood potassium (hypokalemia), and this is more likely at higher doses, when fluid is lost quickly, if you have severe cirrhosis, or after taking the medicine for a long time. Your doctor will check your potassium with blood tests. Tell them if you have muscle cramps, unusual weakness or tiredness, or an irregular heartbeat. Should you eat more potassium while taking hydrochlorothiazide?: Only if your doctor tells you to. Low potassium can sometimes be managed with potassium-rich foods, a potassium supplement, or a different type of diuretic that holds on to potassium. Do not start any of these yourself, because too much potassium can also be harmful, and some people on hydrochlorothiazide do not need extra potassium at all. Is hydrochlorothiazide 12.5mg enough?:

heading: Hydrochlorothiazide FAQ
text: For many people it is. In published trials comparing the two doses, 12.5 mg kept most of the blood pressure reduction seen with 25 mg, and low potassium was consistently less common at 12.5 mg. Starting at 12.5 mg is recommended for adults over 65. Your doctor will decide the right dose for you and may adjust it over time.

heading: Popular FAQ
text: Q: What is the best time of day to take blood pressure medication? A: Research has suggested that taking your blood pressure medication at night instead of in the morning can provide better blood pressure control at night without compromising daytime blood pressure control and reduce your overall risk of dying because of cardiovascular disease by 45%.

heading: What is hydrocodone + acetaminophen?
text: Hydrocodone and acetaminophen is a strong prescription combination pain medicine containing an opioid, hydrocodone, in addition to acetaminophen, which is used to manage moderate to moderately severe pain, when other pain treatments such as non-opioid pain medicines do not treat your pain well enough, or you cannot tolerate them. An opioid pain medicine that can put you at risk for overdose and death. Even if you take your dose correctly as prescribed, you are at risk for opioid addiction, abuse, and misuse that can lead to death. Hydrocodone and acetaminophen is a Schedule II controlled substance. All branded hydrocodone and acetaminophen (Norco, Vicodin, Lortab, Hycet, Lorcet, Verdrocet, Xodol, Zamicet) have been discontinued, but generic hydrocodone and acetaminophen tablets and oral solution is still available. Hydrocodone and acetaminophen first gained FDA approval on May 3, 1982.

heading: Important information about hydrocodone and acetaminophen
text: Get emergency help right away if you take too many hydrocodone and acetaminophen tablets or oral solution (overdose). When you first start taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen, when your dose is changed, or if you take too much (overdose), serious or life-threatening breathing problems that can lead to death may occur. Never give anyone else your hydrocodone and acetaminophen. They could die from taking them. Store hydrocodone and acetaminophen away from children and in a safe place to prevent stealing or abuse. Selling or giving away hydrocodone and acetaminophen products is against the law.

heading: Side Effects
text: Common Side Effects: The possible side effects of hydrocodone and acetaminophen are constipation, nausea, sleepiness, vomiting, tiredness, headache, dizziness, and abdominal pain. Call your healthcare provider if you have any of these symptoms and they are severe. Get emergency medical help if you have: Trouble breathing Shortness of breath Fast heartbeat Chest pain Swelling of your face, tongue, or throat Extreme drowsiness Light-headedness when changing positions Feeling faint Agitation High body temperature Trouble walking Stiff muscles Mental changes such as confusion. These are not all the possible side effects of hydrocodone and acetaminophen. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

heading: Before Taking
text: Do not take hydrocodone and acetaminophen if you have: Severe asthma, trouble breathing, or other lung problems A bowel blockage or a narrowing of the stomach or intestines Signs of an allergy, such as a rash Are allergic to any of its ingredients. Before taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen, tell your healthcare provider if you have a history of: Head injury, seizures Liver, kidney, thyroid problems Problems urinating Pancreas or gallbladder problems Abuse of street or prescription drugs, alcohol addiction, or mental health problems. Tell your healthcare provider if you are: Pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Prolonged use of hydrocodone and acetaminophen during pregnancy can cause withdrawal symptoms in your newborn baby that could be life-threatening if not recognized and treated Breastfeeding. Hydrocodone and acetaminophen pass into breast milk and may harm your baby. Carefully observe infants for increased sleepiness (more than usual), breathing difficulties, or limpness. Seek immediate medical care if you notice these signs. Taking prescription or over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements. Taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen with certain other medicines can cause serious side effects that could lead to death.

heading: How Do I Take Hydrocodone and Acetaminophen
text: When taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen: Do not change your dose. Take hydrocodone and acetaminophen exactly as prescribed by your healthcare provider. Take your prescribed dose every four to six hours at the same time every day. Do not take more than your prescribed dose. If you miss a dose, take your next dose at your usual time. If taking the oral solution, always use a graduated oral syringe or measuring cup to correctly measure your dose. Never use a household teaspoon or tablespoon to measure your medicine. Call your healthcare provider if the dose you are taking does not control your pain, if your pain gets worse, if you feel more sensitive to pain, or if you have new pain. Do not take more medicine without first talking to your healthcare provider. If you have been taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen regularly, do not stop taking it without talking to your healthcare provider. After you stop taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen, flush any unused tablets or oral solution down the toilet.

heading: What Should I Avoid While Taking Hydrocodone and Acetaminophen
text: While taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen, DO NOT: Drive or operate heavy machinery until you know how hydrocodone and acetaminophen affects you. Hydrocodone and acetaminophen can make you sleepy, dizzy, or lightheaded. Drink alcohol or use prescription or over-the-counter medicines that contain alcohol. Using products containing alcohol during treatment with hydrocodone and acetaminophen may cause you to overdose and die.

heading: Dosing Information
text: Adult Dose of Hydrocodone And Acetaminophen for Moderate to Severe Pain: Hydrocodone 2.5 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg per tablet, Hydrocodone 5 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg per tablet: Initial dose: 1 to 2 tablets every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain Maximum dose: 8 tablets/24 hours Hydrocodone 7.5 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg, Hydrocodone 10 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg per tablet: Initial dose: 1 tablet every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain Maximum dose: 6 tablets/24 hours Hydrocodone 7.5 mg-acetaminophen 325 mg per 15 mL oral solution: Initial dose: 15 mL every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain Maximum dose: 90 mL/24 hours Hydrocodone 10 mg-acetaminophen 300 mg per 15 mL oral solution: Initial dose: 11.25 mL every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain Maximum dose: 67.5 mL/24 hours Comments: Doses should be individually titrated to provide adequate analgesia while minimizing adverse reactions. Because of the risks of addiction, abuse, and misuse, the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration consistent with individual patient treatment goals should be used. Monitor patients closely for respiratory depression within the first 24 to 72 hours of initiating therapy and following any increase in dose.

heading: What happens if I overdose?
text: Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. An overdose of acetaminophen and hydrocodone can be fatal. Acute overdosage with hydrocodone and acetaminophen can cause respiratory depression, sleepiness progressing to near-unconsciousness or coma, floppy muscles, cold and clammy skin, constricted pupils, and, in some cases, pulmonary edema, slow heartbeat, low blood pressure, partial or complete airway obstruction, unusual snoring, and death. If the patient who has overdosed becomes very low in oxygen, pupils may become very dilated instead of constricted. Your doctor may recommend that you get naloxone (a medicine to reverse an opioid overdose) and keep it with you at all times. A person caring for you can give the naloxone if you stop breathing or don't wake up. Your caregiver must still get emergency medical help and may need to perform CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) on you while waiting for help to arrive. Anyone can buy naloxone from a pharmacy or local health department. Make sure any person caring for you knows where you keep naloxone and how to use it. The first signs of an acetaminophen overdose include loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, sweating, and confusion or weakness. Later symptoms may include pain in your upper stomach, dark urine, and yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes.

heading: What other drugs will affect hydrocodone and acetaminophen?
text: You may have breathing problems or withdrawal symptoms if you start or stop taking certain other medicines. Tell your doctor if you also use an antibiotic, antifungal medication, heart or blood pressure medication, seizure medication, or medicine to treat HIV or hepatitis C. Opioid medication can interact with many other drugs and cause dangerous side effects or death. Be sure your doctor knows if you also use: cold or allergy medicines, bronchodilator asthma/ COPD medication, or a diuretic ("water pill"); medicines for motion sickness, irritable bowel syndrome, or overactive bladder; other opioids - opioid pain medicine or prescription cough medicine; a sedative like Valium - diazepam, alprazolam, lorazepam, Xanax, Klonopin, Versed, and others; drugs that make you sleepy or slow your breathing - a sleeping pill, muscle relaxer, medicine to treat mood disorders or mental illness; drugs that affect serotonin levels in your body - a stimulant, or medicine for depression, Parkinson's disease, migraine headaches, serious infections, or nausea and vomiting. This list is not complete. Other drugs may interact with acetaminophen and hydrocodone, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Not all possible interactions are listed here. To check for interactions with hydrocodone and acetaminophen, click the link below. Remember, keep this and all other medicines out of the reach of children, never share your medicines with others, and use acetaminophen or hydrocodone only for the indication prescribed.

heading: Popular FAQ
text: Q: What is the difference between Apadaz and Vicodin? A: Vicodin contains a combination of acetaminophen and the opioid hydrocodone, whereas Apadaz is a combination of the prodrug, benzhydrocodone and acetaminophen. When ingested, stomach enzymes cleave the benzhydrocodone prodrug and release the active parent drug hydrocodone.

heading: What is hydroxyzine?
text: Hydroxyzine is a prescription antihistamine used to treat anxiety and tension, itching from allergic skin conditions, and sedation before and after general anesthesia. It comes in three oral forms: Hydroxyzine hydrochloride (HCl) tablets in 10 mg, 25 mg, and 50 mg strengths Hydroxyzine hydrochloride oral solution (a syrup) containing 10 mg in each 5 mL Hydroxyzine pamoate capsules in 25 mg There is also a hydroxyzine hydrochloride injection. It is given into a muscle by a healthcare professional and is never given into a vein or under the skin. Hydroxyzine is not chemically related to benzodiazepines, phenothiazines, reserpine, or meprobamate.

heading: What is hydroxyzine used for?
text: Hydroxyzine taken by mouth is approved for three uses. These are the same for hydroxyzine HCl and hydroxyzine pamoate. Anxiety and tension. For symptomatic relief of anxiety and tension linked to psychoneurosis, and as an add-on treatment in physical illnesses where anxiety is present. Itching from allergic skin conditions. For managing itching (pruritus) caused by allergic conditions such as long-term hives (chronic urticaria), eczema-type rashes, and rashes caused by contact with an irritant. It is also used for itching caused by histamine release. Sedation around surgery. As a sedative given before a procedure (premedication) and after general anesthesia. The injection is also approved for nausea and vomiting and is usually given in hospital or clinic settings. It should not be used for nausea and vomiting caused by pregnancy. text: Avoid driving or hazardous activity until you know how insulin glargine will affect you. Your reactions could be impaired. Avoid medication errors by always checking the medicine label before injecting your insulin. Avoid drinking alcohol or using medicines that contain alcohol. It may interfere with your diabetes treatment.

heading: What other drugs will affect insulin glargine?
text: Many drugs can affect your blood sugar and may also affect insulin glargine. This includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Tell your doctor about all other medicines you use. Not all possible interactions are listed here. Tell your doctor if you also take pioglitazone or rosiglitazone (sometimes contained in combinations with glimepiride or metformin). Taking certain oral diabetes medicines while you are using insulin may increase your risk of serious heart problems.

heading: Popular FAQ
text: Q: How and where should I inject insulin? A: Injecting insulin is not difficult, but it does take a bit of practice. There are three main sites where insulin can be injected: the stomach area except for a 2-inch circle around your navel, and the soft part of your waist, but not anywhere near your spine; the top and outer part of your thighs, but not your inner thighs or anywhere close to your knee; the outer back of your upper arm where there is a pocket of fatty tissue. Q: When is the best time to take Toujeo? A: Toujeo may be given at any time of the day; however, once you have chosen a time, it is best to inject Toujeo within three hours of that time every day. If needed, you can change the time you administer Toujeo, just talk to your doctor about this. Q: How long can Toujeo stay out of the refrigerator? A: Toujeo can stay out of the refrigerator for up to 56 days (8 weeks) according to the prescribing information written on 03/2023. If Toujeo if left out the refrigerator for more than 20 or 30 minutes, it should not be put back into the refrigerator.

heading: Popular FAQ
text: Q: What are the different types of insulin? A: Insulins are usually grouped as fast-acting, intermediate-acting, or long-acting. Within these groups, they can be further classified as human insulin and human insulin analogs. An insulin analog is a human insulin that has one or two amino acids changed which affects how quickly it is absorbed after injection and how fast or slow it acts. Insulin analogs are usually given within 15 minutes of a meal or at the same time as food. Q: Soliqua vs Lantus: What’s the difference between them? A: Soliqua is a combination of insulin glargine plus lixisenatide, and Lantus only contains insulin glargine. Both are once-daily injections that are given under the skin (subcutaneously), but Soliqua can only be used in adults with type 2 diabetes whereas Lantus may be used to treat both type 1 and type 2 diabetes in adults and children over the age of six years. Both are made by Sanofi-Aventis. Q: Can Toujeo be given twice a day? A: Even though Toujeo is usually given once a day, some people may experience better blood sugar control if the dose is split and given twice a day (every 12 hours). Q: How many pens are in a box of Toujeo? A: There are three pens in a box of Toujeo Solostar. There are two pens in a box of Toujeo Max Solostar.

heading: Popular FAQ
text: Q: Is Toujeo a fast or long-acting insulin? A: Toujeo is a long-acting insulin that is usually given once a day. Toujeo lasts for up to 36 hours. Q: What is the difference between Soliqua and Xultophy? A: The main difference between Soliqua and Xultophy is what is inside each pen. Both are once-a-day shots for type 2 diabetes that combine a long-acting (basal) insulin with a GLP-1 medicine. Soliqua 100/33 pairs insulin glargine (Lantus) with lixisenatide (Adlyxin). Xultophy 100/3.6 pairs insulin degludec (Tresiba) with liraglutide (Victoza). They also differ in how and when you inject them, their heart-health data, common side effects, and cost

heading: What is levothyroxine?
text: Levothyroxine is a man-made form of thyroxine (T4), one of the hormones your thyroid gland normally produces. It belongs to a class of medications called hormones, and it works by replacing thyroid hormone that your body is not making enough of. Levothyroxine is used in adults and children, including newborn babies, to: treat hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid - a condition where the thyroid gland does not produce enough thyroid hormone). It replaces the missing hormone whether the condition was present from birth or developed later, and whether the problem starts in the thyroid gland itself or in the pituitary gland or hypothalamus; and lower the level of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in the blood in people being treated for a certain type of thyroid cancer, alongside surgery and radioactive iodine therapy. Levothyroxine injection is used in adults to treat myxedema coma, a rare and life-threatening complication of a severely underactive thyroid. Without thyroid hormone, your body cannot function properly. This may result in poor growth, slow speech, lack of energy, excessive tiredness, constipation, weight gain, hair loss, dry, thick skin, increased sensitivity to cold, joint and muscle pain, heavy or irregular menstrual periods, and depression. When taken correctly, levothyroxine reverses these symptoms, although it may take several weeks before you notice a difference. Levothyroxine is usually taken for life. What levothyroxine is not used for:

heading: What is levothyroxine?
text: Levothyroxine is not used to shrink benign (noncancerous) thyroid nodules or a nontoxic diffuse goiter in people who get enough iodine in their diet. It does not help in these situations, and taking more thyroid hormone than your body needs can cause an overactive thyroid. It is also not used to treat hypothyroidism during the recovery phase of subacute thyroiditis (inflammation of the thyroid gland). Levothyroxine is not used to treat obesity or for weight loss.

heading: Levothyroxine side effects
text: Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to levothyroxine: hives, difficult breathing, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat. Allergic reactions are usually caused by the inactive ingredients in a product rather than by levothyroxine itself, so your doctor may suggest trying a different brand or form. Levothyroxine may cause serious side effects. Call your doctor at once if you have: sudden pain or trouble moving your hip, wrist, or back; fast or irregular heartbeats, or a pounding heartbeat; chest pain, pain spreading to your jaw or shoulder; wheezing or shortness of breath; swelling in your legs or ankles, or new or worsening breathlessness when lying down; fever, swollen glands, itching, joint pain, or not feeling well; nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea; confusion or feeling disoriented; a seizure; or high blood sugar - increased thirst, increased urination, dry mouth, fruity breath odor. Common levothyroxine side effects may include: fever, hot flashes, increased sweating, feeling too hot; tiredness; skin rash, flushing, hair loss; chest pain, fast or irregular heartbeats, shortness of breath; headache, leg cramps, muscle cramps, muscle pain or weakness; tremors, feeling nervous, anxious, irritable, or emotional, sleep problems (insomnia); increased or change in appetite; weight loss or weight gain; changes in your menstrual periods, or difficulty getting pregnant; or stomach cramps, vomiting, diarrhea.

heading: Levothyroxine side effects
text: Most of these side effects happen when the levothyroxine dose is higher than your body needs, which produces symptoms of an overactive thyroid. Tell your doctor if you have any of them so your dose can be checked. Side effects in children: Children taking levothyroxine may also develop increased pressure around the brain (which can cause headaches, vomiting, or vision changes) or a hip problem called slipped capital femoral epiphysis, which causes hip, groin, or knee pain and limping. Call your child's doctor about any of these symptoms. Too much levothyroxine in babies can cause the soft spots on the skull to close too early, and in older children it can cause the growth plates to close too early, which may reduce final adult height. Too little levothyroxine can affect a child's learning and growth. This is why children need regular blood tests and check-ups. This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
