heading: Warnings
text: Levothyroxine should not be used to treat obesity or weight problems. Dangerous side effects or death can occur from the misuse of this medicine, especially if you are taking any other weight-loss medications or appetite suppressants. Taking more than your recommended dose will not make this medicine more effective, and may cause serious side effects. Levothyroxine has a narrow therapeutic index, which means the difference between too little and too much is small. Taking too much or too little over time can affect your heart, bones, blood sugar, cholesterol, digestion, memory and concentration, fertility, and, in children, growth and development. Your doctor will start you on a suitable dose and adjust it gradually based on blood tests. You may not be able to use levothyroxine if you have certain medical conditions. Tell your doctor if you have an untreated or uncontrolled adrenal gland disorder or any heart problems such as a recent heart attack. If you have an adrenal gland problem, you will need to start treatment with a steroid (glucocorticoid) medicine before you start levothyroxine. Starting levothyroxine first can trigger a sudden, serious drop in adrenal hormones known as an adrenal crisis. Older adults and people with heart disease are usually started on a lower dose, because too much thyroid hormone can cause an irregular heartbeat (most commonly atrial fibrillation), angina, or other heart problems. Tell your doctor if you develop chest pain, breathlessness, or a fast or irregular heartbeat.

heading: Warnings
text: Taking more levothyroxine than your body needs over a long period can weaken your bones and lead to a higher risk of fractures. This is more likely after menopause. Your doctor will aim to give you the lowest dose that controls your thyroid levels. Oral levothyroxine should not be used to treat myxedema coma. Levothyroxine given into a vein is used instead.

heading: Before taking this medicine
text: You should not use levothyroxine if you have an untreated or uncontrolled adrenal gland disorder. You should not use certain liquid or injectable forms of levothyroxine if you are allergic to glycerin or edetate disodium. To make sure this medicine is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had: a thyroid nodule; thyroiditis (inflammation of the thyroid gland); heart problems such as a heart attack, stroke, angina, or an irregular heartbeat; a blood clot or a blood clotting disorder; diabetes (your diabetes medicine may need to be adjusted); anemia (low red blood cells); weak bones (osteoporosis), or low bone mineral density; problems with your pituitary or adrenal gland; an allergy to any food or drugs; recently received radiation therapy with iodine (such as I-131); or kidney disease. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. Having hypothyroidism during pregnancy may increase the risk of miscarriage, high blood pressure in pregnancy, pre-eclampsia, stillbirth, or premature birth, and untreated hypothyroidism can affect the baby's brain development. The benefit of treating hypothyroidism outweighs these risks, and levothyroxine should not be stopped during pregnancy. Your dose needs are often higher during pregnancy. Your doctor will check your thyroid blood tests as soon as your pregnancy is confirmed and at least once in each trimester, and will usually put you back on your pre-pregnancy dose straight after you give birth, with another blood test 4 to 8 weeks later.

heading: Before taking this medicine
text: Tell your doctor if you are breastfeeding. Levothyroxine passes into breast milk, but no harmful effects on breastfed babies have been reported. Treating hypothyroidism properly may also help milk supply if it is low. Your dose needs may be different while you are nursing. You may be more likely to have a broken bone while using levothyroxine, particularly if your dose is higher than you need. Talk with your doctor about ways to keep your bones healthy.

heading: How should I use levothyroxine?
text: Take levothyroxine exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose. Some brands of levothyroxine have different dosage instructions and/or recommendations of how soon you need to take them before eating food. Always check the instructions on the label. Oral levothyroxine: Oral levothyroxine is taken by mouth and is available as tablets, capsules, and an oral solution. Keep using this medicine even if you feel well. It may take 4 to 6 weeks to get the full benefit of a dose. You will need frequent medical tests, and your next dose may be delayed based on the results. This medicine can affect the results of certain medical tests. Tell any doctor who treats you that you are using this medicine. Tell your doctor if you have a planned surgery or dental procedure. Taking more than your recommended dose will not make this medicine more effective, and may cause serious side effects. Tablets and capsules: Take levothyroxine tablets and capsules on an empty stomach, at least 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast with a full glass of water. A full glass of water is important to avoid choking or gagging, because the tablet can start to break apart quickly. Take the medicine at the same time each day. Swallow the capsule whole and do not crush, chew, break, or open it. Tell your doctor if your child cannot swallow a capsule whole.

heading: How should I use levothyroxine?
text: If you cannot swallow a tablet whole, crush the tablet and mix it with 1 or 2 teaspoons of water; give the mixture right away by spoon or dropper and make sure all of it is taken. Do not save it for later use. Do not mix it into soy-based infant formula or other foods that can stop levothyroxine being absorbed. Keep each tablet or capsule in the blister pack until you are ready to take one. Store at room temperature away from moisture, heat, and light. Oral solution (liquid medicine): Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device (not a kitchen spoon). Dosages are based on weight in children and teenagers. Your child's dose may change if the child gains or loses weight. Your dose needs may change if you switch to a different brand, strength, or form of levothyroxine. Avoid medication errors by using only the medicine your doctor prescribes. Tirosint-Sol oral solution comes in single-dose ampules and can be administered 15 minutes before eating breakfast. Squeeze the liquid directly into your mouth, onto a spoon, or into a glass of water to drink right away. Use all ampules within 3 months after opening the foil pouch. Ermeza and Thyquidity liquids should be taken on an empty stomach, at least 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast. Store them in their original bottle. Use Ermeza within 90 days and Thyquidity within 8 weeks of opening the bottle. Store at room temperature away from moisture, heat, and light. Intravenous levothyroxine:

heading: How should I use levothyroxine?
text: This is given as an injection into a vein by a healthcare provider and should only be used to treat myxedema coma. Blood tests, biotin, and monitoring: Your doctor will use blood tests to check that your dose is right, usually 6 to 8 weeks after any dose change, and then every 6 to 12 months once your dose is stable. Children are tested more often, including 2 and 4 weeks after starting treatment and 2 weeks after any dose change. Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you take biotin, or a multivitamin, hair, skin, or nail supplement that contains biotin (sometimes listed as vitamin B7). Biotin can interfere with thyroid blood tests and give a falsely high or falsely low result, which could lead to the wrong dose change. Stop biotin and any biotin-containing supplements at least 2 days before a thyroid blood test. If your symptoms and blood tests still suggest an underactive thyroid even though you are on a dose that should be enough, it may be because the medicine is not being absorbed properly, doses are being missed, or another medicine is interfering. Talk to your doctor before your dose is increased.

heading: What happens if I miss a dose?
text: In a medical setting, you are not likely to miss a dose of levothyroxine injection. Take the missed oral levothyroxine dose as soon as you remember, and then go back to your regular schedule. Do not use two doses at one time.

heading: What happens if I overdose?
text: Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. An overdose can be fatal. Overdose symptoms may include headache, leg cramps, tremors, feeling nervous or irritable, confusion, chest pain, shortness of breath, fast or pounding heartbeats, stroke, seizures, shock, and coma. Symptoms may not appear straight away and can take several days to develop, so get medical advice even if the person seems well.

heading: What should I avoid while using levothyroxine?
text: Avoid the following food products within 1 hour of taking oral levothyroxine or the medication will not be as effective: grapefruit juice, infant soy formula, soybean flour, cottonseed meal, walnuts, and high-fiber foods. Grapefruit juice can both delay absorption and reduce the amount of levothyroxine that gets into your body. If you eat or drink any of these regularly, tell your doctor, as your dose may need adjusting.

heading: What other drugs will affect levothyroxine?
text: Sometimes it is not safe to use certain medicines at the same time. Some drugs can affect your thyroid hormone levels and also make levothyroxine less effective. If you use any of the following drugs, avoid taking them within 4 hours before or 4 hours after you use levothyroxine: calcium carbonate (Alka-Mints, Caltrate, Os-Cal, Oyster Shell Calcium, Rolaids Soft Chew, Tums, and others); sevelamer, lanthanum; cholestyramine, colesevelam, colestipol; iron supplements, including ferrous sulfate; sucralfate; sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kalexate, Kayexalate, Kionex); stomach acid reducers - esomeprazole, lansoprazole, omeprazole, rabeprazole, Nexium, Prilosec, Prevacid, Protonix, Zegerid, and others (this applies to most brands of levothyroxine except for Tirosint-SOL); or antacids that contain aluminum or magnesium - Gaviscon, Maalox, Milk of Magnesia, Mintox, Mylanta, Pepcid Complete, and others. Tell your doctor about all your other medicines, especially: orlistat; phenobarbital, rifampin; ketamine, steroid medicines such as dexamethasone; antidepressants such as amitriptyline, maprotiline, or sertraline; heart or blood pressure medication, including amiodarone, digoxin, propranolol, and other beta blockers; furosemide given by injection; seizure medicines such as carbamazepine or phenytoin; high-dose aspirin, or anti-inflammatory painkillers; estrogen, birth control pills, or tamoxifen; testosterone or anabolic steroids; diabetes medications, including insulin; cancer medicine such as imatinib; biotin or supplements that contain biotin; or a blood thinner - warfarin, Coumadin, Jantoven.

heading: What other drugs will affect levothyroxine?
text: If you have diabetes, levothyroxine can raise your blood sugar, and you may need more of your diabetes medicine or insulin. Check your blood sugar more often when you start, change, or stop levothyroxine, and tell your doctor about any changes. If you take a blood thinner such as warfarin, levothyroxine can increase its effect. You may need more frequent blood clotting tests and a lower blood thinner dose. This list is not complete, and many other drugs may interact with levothyroxine. This includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Not all possible drug interactions are listed here.

heading: Popular FAQ
text: Q: Does levothyroxine cause weight gain or loss? A: In most cases, levothyroxine causes some weight loss. According to the American Thyroid Association, when this medication is started, you may lose up to 10% of your weight. This weight is mainly water weight, since being hypothyroid makes you retain water. Q: What can I eat for breakfast after taking levothyroxine? A: Most foods are considered fine to eat for breakfast as long as they are eaten 30 to 60 minutes after taking levothyroxine. Levothyroxine should be taken once a day on an empty stomach in the morning. Q: Can I take other medications with levothyroxine? A: Levothyroxine is known to interact with many other medications (called a drug-drug interaction), but there are different kinds of drug-drug interactions. Some interactions require that drugs not be taken at the same time, while other interactions require more frequent laboratory testing or monitoring of your disease symptoms. Q: How soon after taking levothyroxine can I take omeprazole? A: There is a known drug interaction between levothyroxine and omeprazole, but the timing of when you take the two medicines is not relevant. Omeprazole decreases the absorption of your thyroid medication. If you need to be on a course of omeprazole while taking levothyroxine, your doctor may order more frequent laboratory testing to confirm you are absorbing enough levothyroxine.

heading: Popular FAQ
text: Q: Does levothyroxine cause hair loss? A: Yes, levothyroxine, the main treatment for a sluggish thyroid gland, may cause hair loss in addition to other side effects. You may experience partial hair loss in the first few months of treatment, but this often resolves and goes back to normal in a short time. Q: How long after taking levothyroxine can you drink milk? A: You should avoid drinking milk until at least 4 hours after taking levothyroxine. Dairy products—including milk, cheese and yogurt—contain high calcium levels, which affect how levothyroxine is absorbed into your body. Q: How long does levothyroxine stay in your system? A: Levothyroxine will stay in your system for around 4 to 6 weeks. It takes longer for people with hypothyroidism to eliminate levothyroxine (closer to 6 weeks) than those with normal thyroid function. Q: What is the difference between Levoxyl and Synthroid? A: Levoxyl and Synthroid are brand names for the drug levothyroxine. Both medications contain the same active ingredient, levothyroxine, but they contain different inactive ingredients. Q: Can you take thyroid supplements with levothyroxine? A: Taking any other medication or supplement with levothyroxine may cause you to need a higher or lower dose of levothyroxine. Even supplements like calcium or iron can affect absorption of levothyroxine.

heading: What is lisinopril?
text: Lisinopril is used alone or in combination with other medications to treat high blood pressure in adults and children 6 years of age and older. Lisinopril is also used in adults to treat congestive heart failure and to improve survival after a heart attack. Lisinopril belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors. It works by decreasing certain chemicals that tighten the blood vessels, so blood flows more smoothly and the heart can pump blood more efficiently. High blood pressure is a common condition and when not treated, can cause damage to the brain, heart, blood vessels, kidneys, and other parts of the body. Damage to these organs may cause heart disease, a heart attack, heart failure, stroke, kidney failure, loss of vision, and other problems. In addition to taking medication, making lifestyle changes will also help to control your blood pressure. These changes include eating a diet that is low in fat and salt, maintaining a healthy weight, exercising at least 30 minutes most days, not smoking, and using alcohol in moderation.

heading: Warnings
text: Do not use lisinopril if you are pregnant. It could harm the unborn baby. Stop using this medicine and tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. You should not use this medicine if you have ever had angioedema. Do not take lisinopril within 36 hours before or after taking medicine that contains sacubitril (such as Entresto). If you have diabetes, do not use lisinopril together with any medication that contains aliskiren (such as Amturnide, Tekturna, Tekamlo). You may also need to avoid taking lisinopril with aliskiren if you have kidney disease.

heading: Before taking this medicine
text: You should not use lisinopril if you are allergic to it or to any other ACE (angiotensin converting enzyme) inhibitor such as captopril, fosinopril, enalapril, benazepril, moexipril, perindopril, quinapril, ramipril, or trandolapril. Do not take lisinopril within 36 hours before or after taking medicine that contains sacubitril (such as Entresto). If you have diabetes, do not take lisinopril with any medication that contains aliskiren (a blood pressure medicine). Do not take lisinopril if you have a history of angioedema (severe allergic reaction). To make sure this medicine is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had: heart disease, heart problems such as a recent heart attack; low blood pressure; low white blood cell count; stomach pain; if you are on a low-salt diet; diabetes; liver disease; or kidney disease (or if you are on dialysis). You may also need to avoid taking lisinopril with aliskiren if you have kidney disease. Stop using this medicine and tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. Lisinopril can cause injury or death to the unborn baby if you use the medicine during your second or third trimester. Do not breastfeed.

heading: How should I take lisinopril?
text: Take lisinopril exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.. You may take lisinopril with or without food. Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device (not a kitchen spoon). Your blood pressure will need to be checked often and you may need frequent blood tests. Tell your doctor if you have a planned surgery. Call your doctor if you have ongoing vomiting or diarrhea, or if you are sweating more than usual. You can easily become dehydrated while taking lisinopril. This can lead to very low blood pressure, an electrolyte imbalance, or kidney failure. If you have high blood pressure, keep using lisinopril even if you feel well. High blood pressure often has no symptoms. Store tightly closed at room temperature, away from moisture and heat. Do not freeze.

heading: Dosing information
text: Usual Adult Dose for Hypertension: Initial dose: 10 mg orally once a day; 5 mg orally once a day Maintenance dose: 20 to 40 mg orally once a day Maximum dose: 80 mg orally once a day Comments: -The initial dose is 5 mg orally once a day in patients receiving a diuretic. -The 80 mg dose is used but does not appear to give greater effect. -If blood pressure is not controlled with lisinopril alone, a low dose of a diuretic may be added (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide, 12.5 mg). After the addition of a diuretic, it may be possible to reduce the dose of lisinopril. Usual Adult Dose for Congestive Heart Failure: Initial dose: 2.5 to 5 mg orally once a day Maintenance dose: Dosage should be increased as tolerated Maximum dose: 40 mg orally once a day Comments: -The diuretic dose may need to be adjusted to help minimize hypovolemia, which may contribute to hypotension. The appearance of hypotension after the initial dose of lisinopril does not preclude subsequent careful dose titration with the drug. Usual Adult Dose for Myocardial Infarction:

heading: Dosing information
text: Initial dose: 5 mg orally (within 24 hours of the onset of acute myocardial infarction) Subsequent doses: 5 mg orally after 24 hours, then 10 mg orally after 48 hours. Maintenance dose: 10 mg orally once a day. Dosing should continue for at least 6 weeks. Comments: -Therapy should be initiated at 2.5 mg in patients with a low systolic blood pressure (less than or equal to 120 mm Hg and greater than 100 mmHg) during the first 3 days after the infarct. If prolonged hypotension occurs (systolic blood pressure less than 90 mmHg for more than 1 hour) therapy should be withdrawn. Uses: Reduction of mortality in acute myocardial infarction Usual Adult Dose for Diabetic Nephropathy: Initial dose: 10 to 20 mg orally once a day Maintenance dose: 20 to 40 mg orally once a day Dosage may be titrated upward every 3 days Comments: -Not an approved indication. Usual Geriatric Dose for Hypertension: Initial dose: 2.5 to 5 mg orally once a day Maintenance dose: Dosages should be increased at 2.5 mg to 5 mg per day at 1 to 2 week intervals. Maximum dose: 40 mg orally once a day Usual Pediatric Dose for Hypertension:

heading: Dosing information
text: Pediatric patients greater than or equal to 6 years of age: Initial dose: 0.07 mg/kg orally once a day (Maximum initial dose is 5 mg once a day) Maintenance dose: Dosage should be adjusted according to blood pressure response at 1 to 2 week intervals. text: Talk to your healthcare provider if you are breastfeeding or plan to breastfeed. Metformin can pass into your breast milk. Your healthcare provider will be able to advise you about the best way to feed your baby while you take this medicine.

heading: How should I take metformin?
text: Take metformin exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose. Use the medicine exactly as directed. Take metformin with a meal, unless your doctor tells you otherwise. Some forms of metformin are taken only once daily with the evening meal. Follow your doctor's instructions. Take immediate release tablets in divided doses 2 to 3 times a day with meals. Your dose will be increased slowly to minimise gastrointestinal side effects. Do not crush, chew, or break an extended-release tablet. Swallow it whole. Measure liquid medicine carefully. Shake the oral suspension before you measure a dose. Use the dosing syringe provided, or use a medicine dose-measuring device (not a kitchen spoon). Some tablets are made with a shell that is not absorbed or melted in the body. Part of this shell may appear in your stool. This is normal and will not make the medicine less effective. You may have low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) and feel very hungry, dizzy, irritable, confused, anxious, or shaky. To quickly treat hypoglycemia, eat or drink a fast-acting source of sugar (fruit juice, hard candy, crackers, raisins, or non-diet soda). Your doctor may prescribe a glucagon injection kit in case you have severe hypoglycemia. Be sure your family or close friends know how to give you this injection in an emergency.

heading: How should I take metformin?
text: Blood sugar levels can be affected by stress, illness, surgery, exercise, alcohol use, or skipping meals. Ask your doctor before changing your dose or medication schedule. Metformin is only part of a complete treatment program that may also include diet, exercise, weight control, regular blood sugar testing, and special medical care. Follow your doctor's instructions very closely. Store at room temperature away from moisture, heat, and light. Your doctor may have you take extra vitamin B12 while you are taking this medicine. Take only the amount of vitamin B12 that your doctor has prescribed.

heading: What happens if I miss a dose?

heading: What happens if I overdose?

heading: What to avoid
text: Avoid drinking alcohol. It lowers blood sugar and may increase your risk of lactic acidosis.

heading: What other drugs will affect metformin?
text: Many drugs can interact with metformin; this includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Not all possible interactions are listed here. Tell your doctor about all your current medicines and any medicine you start or stop using. Medicines that have a carbonic anhydrase inhibiting effect like topiramate (often used for seizures or migraines), zonisamide (used for seizures), acetazolamide (used for glaucoma, altitude sickness, and other conditions), and dichlorphenamide (used for a muscle condition called periodic paralysis) can raise the risk of a rare but serious condition called lactic acidosis when taken with metformin. These medicines commonly lower a substance in your blood called bicarbonate, which your body needs to keep its acid levels balanced. If you're taking metformin along with any of these medicines, your doctor may want to monitor you more closely. Other medicines that may increase risk of lactic acidosis. Some medicines including cimetidine (used for heartburn), ranolazine (used for chest pain/angina), dolutegravir (used to treat HIV), and vandetanib (used to treat certain thyroid cancers) can all cause metformin levels to increase. They do this by blocking the same pathway your kidneys use to clear metformin out of your system. Since higher metformin levels raise the risk of lactic acidosis, your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks before prescribing any of these together with metformin.

heading: What other drugs will affect metformin?
text: Insulin or other diabetes medicines that raise insulin (like sulfonylureas): Combining these with metformin can lower your blood sugar too much. Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you're taking more than one diabetes medicine. Alcohol: Drinking alcohol, especially in large amounts or regularly, can make it harder for your body to process metformin normally and raises the risk of lactic acidosis. Contrast dye used in imaging tests (like CT scans): This type of dye can temporarily affect kidney function, which can let metformin build up in your body. Your doctor may have you stop taking metformin around the time of the test and restart it once your kidney function is confirmed to be back to normal.

heading: Metformin for Weight Loss: What the Research Shows
text: Does metformin work for weight loss?: Yes. Metformin can lead to a modest weight loss, though results vary, and it's generally smaller amount of weight loss than what's seen with medications specifically approved for weight loss. In the landmark Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP), a randomized controlled trial in people at high risk for diabetes, participants taking metformin lost more weight than those on placebo. Metformin patients lost 2.7% of body weight after one year, compared to 0.43% for placebo, and 2.1% after two years compared to essentially no change (0.02%) for placebo. Looking at it another way, 29% of people on metformin lost at least 5% of their starting body weight after one year, versus just 13% on placebo, a gap that held up at the two-year mark (26% vs. 14%). Metformin is not FDA-approved for weight loss.

heading: How does metformin help PCOS?
text: Metformin is prescribed to manage polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) because it improves how the body responds to insulin. PCOS affects about 1 in 10 women of reproductive age and is often marked by insulin resistance, in which the body doesn't respond well to insulin, prompting the pancreas to produce more. This excess insulin drives up androgen (male hormone) production, worsening symptoms like irregular periods, infertility, acne, and excess hair growth. Metformin helps by lowering insulin levels, decreasing the liver's glucose production, improving glucose uptake by muscles, and reducing circulating androgen levels as well, which can support more regular ovulation and menstrual cycles. Although metformin is not FDA-approved to treat PCOS, it's widely prescribed as an off-label treatment, particularly for those with insulin resistance or fertility difficulties, and it's backed by extensive research and clinical guidelines. Beyond helping regulate cycles and support ovulation, metformin may also help reduce androgen-related symptoms such as acne and excess hair growth, and can aid with weight management for those affected by PCOS-related weight gain.

heading: Popular FAQ
text: Q: When is the best time to take metformin? A: Metformin should be taken after having a meal or eating food, especially when you are first starting treatment. This can help reduce any stomach side effects. Q: Can you take metformin and Ozempic together? A: Yes, metformin and Ozempic (semaglutide) are often used together under a healthcare provider’s guidance to manage type 2 diabetes. They work through different mechanisms to lower blood sugar and may also help with weight management, but both have specific safety considerations such as Ozempic’s boxed thyroid warning and metformin’s kidney function requirements. Q: How long does metformin take to work? A: Metformin will usually start lowering your blood sugar (glucose) levels in the first week of treatment, but it may take 2 to 3 months to see its full effect. Metformin is a preferred initial oral treatment for people with type 2 diabetes, and is usually taken on a long-term basis. It may be combined with other blood glucose-lowering treatments, if needed. Q: What is the safest diabetes medication? A: Metformin is widely considered the safest first-line medication for type 2 diabetes. With decades of clinical use and extensive safety data, it remains the preferred initial treatment according to the American Diabetes Association (ADA). However, the safest medication for any individual depends on their specific health profile, age, kidney function, and treatment goals.

heading: Popular FAQ
text: Q: Why does metformin cause diarrhea? A: Metformin causes diarrhea by changing gut bacteria, affecting bile acid absorption, blocking water absorption in the intestines, and increasing gut-stimulating hormones. These combined effects make stools looser and more frequent. Q: Can you take metformin without food? A: If you take metformin without food you may end up with an upset stomach, especially if you are just starting treatment. Nausea and vomiting are some of the most common side effects with metformin and can occur in over 30% of patients. Q: Does metformin lower A1C, if so how much? A: When metformin is used alone as a single agent, it lowers A1C by about 1 to 1.5 percentage points (1-1.5%) on average, at standard therapeutic doses. A1C is a measure of longer-term blood sugar control. In most patients, metformin is suggested as the initial treatment for type 2 diabetes, but its glucose-lowering effect may not be adequate for all patients if used alone. Q: Does metformin cause weight loss? A: Metformin is generally considered weight neutral or modestly weight reducing, with average losses around 1–3 kg (2–7 lb) over several months in people with type 2 diabetes or obesity. Many people lose little or no weight, and the effect varies widely between individuals.

heading: Popular FAQ
text: Q: What are the symptoms of Metformin related lactic acidosis? A: Signs or symptoms of lactic acidosis may include feeling very weak or tired, unusual muscle pain or weakness, unusual sleepiness, trouble breathing, stomach discomfort, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, feeling cold, dizziness, and changes in your heartbeat.

heading: What is methylphenidate?
text: Methylphenidate is a central nervous system stimulant. It affects chemicals in the brain and nerves that contribute to hyperactivity and impulse control. Methylphenidate is used to treat attention deficit disorder (ADD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and narcolepsy. Methylphenidate should be used as a part of a total treatment program for ADHD that may include counseling or other therapies.

heading: Warnings
text: Methylphenidate may be habit-forming. Misuse can cause addiction, overdose, or death. Tell your doctor if you have had problems with drug or alcohol abuse. Stimulants have caused stroke, heart attack, and sudden death in people with high blood pressure, heart disease, or a heart defect. Do not use methylphenidate if you have used an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days, such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, or tranylcypromine. Methylphenidate may cause new or worsening psychosis (unusual thoughts or behavior), especially if you have a history of depression, mental illness, or bipolar disorder. You may have blood circulation problems that can cause numbness, pain, or discoloration in your fingers or toes. Call your doctor right away if you have: signs of heart problems - chest pain, feeling light-headed or short of breath; signs of psychosis - paranoia, aggression, new behavior problems, seeing or hearing things that are not real; signs of circulation problems - unexplained wounds on your fingers or toes. Tell your doctor if you have a history of drug or alcohol addiction. Keep the medication where others cannot get to it.

heading: Popular FAQ
text: Q: What is metilfenidato used for? A: Metilfenidato is the Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese translation for methylphenidate which may be used to treat children or adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) to help with hyperactivity and impulsive behavior, and allow them to concentrate better. Metilfenidato may also be used to treat adults with narcolepsy. Metilfenidato translates to methylphenidate.

heading: What is metoprolol?
text: Metoprolol is a beta-blocker medication used to treat high blood pressure, chest pain (angina), and heart failure, and to improve survival after a heart attack. It works mainly on the heart, so it is called a cardioselective beta-blocker. Metoprolol works by blocking the effect of adrenaline and noradrenaline on beta-1 receptors in your heart. This slows your heart rate, reduces how hard your heart squeezes, and lowers your blood pressure. Because the heart is doing less work, it needs less oxygen, which is why metoprolol also helps with angina. Exactly how metoprolol works for high blood pressure, heart failure, and after a heart attack is not fully understood. At higher blood levels, metoprolol also blocks beta-2 receptors in the airways and blood vessels, which is why it still needs care in people with breathing problems. Metoprolol comes as two different salts, metoprolol tartrate and metoprolol succinate. They are not interchangeable dose for dose: Metoprolol tartrate, an immediate-release tablet usually taken once or twice a day (brand name Lopressor) Metoprolol succinate, an extended-release tablet or capsule taken once a day (brand names Toprol-XL and Kapspargo Sprinkle) Metoprolol tartrate is also given as an injection into a vein in a hospital during a heart attack.

heading: What is metoprolol used for?
text: Metoprolol is FDA-approved to treat high blood pressure, angina, heart failure, and heart attack, but the two forms are not approved for the same conditions. Condition | Metoprolol tartrate (immediate release) | Metoprolol succinate (extended release) High blood pressure (hypertension) in adults | Yes | Yes High blood pressure in children 6 years and older | No | Yes Angina (chest pain) | Yes | Yes Heart failure | No | Yes Heart attack (myocardial infarction) | Yes | No High blood pressure (hypertension). Lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of fatal and non-fatal heart and blood vessel events, mainly strokes and heart attacks. Metoprolol can be used on its own or with other blood pressure medicines. Many people need more than one medicine to reach their blood pressure goal. Angina. Metoprolol is used for long-term treatment of angina, to reduce how often attacks happen and to help you do more before chest pain starts. It is not used to stop an attack that has already begun. Heart failure. Only the extended-release form is approved for heart failure. It is used to reduce the risk of dying from heart and blood vessel causes and to reduce hospital admissions for heart failure.

heading: What is metoprolol used for?
text: Heart attack (myocardial infarction). Metoprolol tartrate is used in people whose blood pressure and circulation are stable after a definite or suspected heart attack, to reduce the risk of dying from heart and blood vessel causes. In hospital, it may be started as an injection into a vein and then continued as tablets.

heading: What is the difference between metoprolol succinate and metoprolol tartrate?
text: The two forms release the same medicine at different speeds, and they are approved for different conditions. Metoprolol tartrate is released all at once, so it acts sooner and wears off sooner. Metoprolol succinate is released slowly over the day, so one dose lasts about 24 hours. Only the extended-release form is approved for heart failure and for children, and only the immediate-release form is approved for use after a heart attack. heading: Metoprolol side effects
text: The most common side effects of metoprolol are tiredness, dizziness, low mood (depression), diarrhea, shortness of breath, a slow heartbeat (bradycardia), and itching or rash. Most side effects reported in studies were mild and did not last. Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to metoprolol: hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat. Common side effects of metoprolol: In studies of people taking metoprolol for high blood pressure or angina: Tiredness and dizziness occurred in about 10% of people Low mood or depression was reported in about 5 out of 100 people Diarrhea occurred in about 5% of people Itching or rash occurred in about 5% of people Shortness of breath and a slow heartbeat occurred in about 3% of people Cold hands and feet, palpitations, swelling of the ankles, and low blood pressure were each reported in about 1% of people Nausea, dry mouth, stomach pain, constipation, gas, and heartburn were each reported in about 1% of people Headache, nightmares, trouble sleeping, confusion, and short-term memory loss have also been reported. In the heart failure study of extended-release metoprolol, dizziness or vertigo was reported by 1.8% of people taking metoprolol compared with 1.0% taking placebo, and a slow heartbeat by 1.5% compared with 0.4%. Other reported side effects: These have been reported since metoprolol came on the market. Their frequency is not known: Hair thinning or hair loss, which reversed after stopping

text: Reduced sex drive and difficulty getting an erection Dry eyes, blurred vision, and ringing in the ears Sweating, sensitivity to sunlight, and worsening of psoriasis Change in taste, joint and muscle pain, and fainting Liver inflammation (hepatitis) A severe drop in white blood cells (agranulocytosis), which can show up as fever, chills, or a sore throat Serious side effects of metoprolol: Some of these, such as shortness of breath and a slow heartbeat, are also listed as common side effects above. They need urgent attention when they are severe, new, or getting worse. Call your doctor at once if you have: A very slow heartbeat, pauses in your heartbeat, or a feeling that you might faint. Sinus pause, heart block, and cardiac arrest have all been reported. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

heading: Metoprolol warnings
text: The most important warning with metoprolol is not to stop it suddenly. Stopping a beta blocker abruptly can bring on worse chest pain and, in some cases, a heart attack. If your treatment needs to stop, your prescriber will lower the dose gradually over 1 to 2 weeks and watch how you respond. This applies even if you only take metoprolol for blood pressure, because heart disease is common and is not always known about. Talk to your care team before starting metoprolol if any of these apply to you. Asthma or other breathing problems. Beta blockers can tighten the airways. Metoprolol is used in people with these conditions only when other treatments are not suitable, at the lowest possible dose, with a reliever inhaler on hand. Heart failure. Heart failure can get worse while the dose is being increased. Tell your doctor about weight gain or increasing breathlessness. A slow heart rate or a conduction problem in the heart. This includes first-degree heart block, sinus node problems, and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. Your heart rate should be monitored. Diabetes or long gaps without food. Metoprolol can hide the early warning signs of low blood sugar, such as a fast heartbeat, and can make low blood sugar more severe or last longer. The risk is higher if you are fasting, not eating regularly, or vomiting. An overactive thyroid. Metoprolol can mask signs of an overactive thyroid. Stopping it suddenly can trigger a thyroid crisis.

heading: Metoprolol warnings
text: Circulation problems in your arms or legs. Beta blockers can make symptoms of poor circulation worse. A history of severe allergic reactions. If you have anaphylaxis while taking a beta blocker, the usual dose of injectable epinephrine may not work as well. Pheochromocytoma (a tumor of the adrenal gland). Metoprolol must only be started after an alpha blocker has been started, or blood pressure can rise sharply. Liver disease. Metoprolol is broken down by the liver, so levels can build up. Treatment is usually started at a lower dose. Surgery. Tell your surgeon and dentist that you take metoprolol. Long-term beta blocker treatment is not usually stopped before surgery. Starting a high dose of extended-release metoprolol shortly before non-cardiac surgery is avoided, because in one large trial this was linked to more slow heartbeats, low blood pressure, strokes, and deaths.

heading: Who should not take metoprolol?
text: You should not take metoprolol if you have a very slow heart rate, heart block beyond the first degree, sick sinus syndrome without a pacemaker, cardiogenic shock, or heart failure that is not under control. Metoprolol is not for you if you have: Severe bradycardia (a very slow heart rate) Second-degree or third-degree heart block, which is a fault in the heart's electrical signal Sick sinus syndrome, unless you have a permanent pacemaker Cardiogenic shock, when the heart cannot pump enough blood Decompensated heart failure, meaning heart failure that is not stable An allergy to metoprolol or to any of the other ingredients in your product Immediate-release metoprolol tartrate tablets should also not be used if your top blood pressure reading is below 100 mmHg.

heading: Before taking metoprolol
text: Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you: Take any other medicine for your heart or blood pressure, especially digoxin, clonidine, diltiazem, or verapamil Take fluoxetine, paroxetine, quinidine, or propafenone, which raise metoprolol levels in your blood Are pregnant, planning a pregnancy, or breastfeeding Have liver problems Have ever had a severe allergic reaction to anything, including foods and insect stings Kidney problems do not usually change your dose. The amount of metoprolol in your body and how long it lasts are not meaningfully different in people with kidney failure.

heading: How should I take metoprolol?
text: Take metoprolol at the same time each day, exactly as prescribed. Do not change your dose or stop taking it without talking to your prescriber first. Immediate-release metoprolol tartrate tablets should be taken with a meal or immediately after a meal. For extended-release tablets and capsules, taking your dose with or just after a meal is preferred, but food does not have a significant effect on how much metoprolol your body absorbs. Keep taking metoprolol even if you feel well. High blood pressure often causes no symptoms. Extended-release tablets are scored and can be split in half if your prescriber tells you to. Swallow the whole or half tablet without crushing or chewing it. Extended-release capsules (Kapspargo Sprinkle) should be swallowed whole. If you cannot swallow the capsule, you can open it and sprinkle the contents over a teaspoon of soft food such as applesauce, pudding, or yogurt. Swallow the mixture within 60 minutes and do not save any for later. Tell your doctor if you are fasting or vomiting, because this raises your risk of low blood sugar. Your blood pressure and heart rate will need checking regularly. Store metoprolol at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C), away from moisture and heat. Metoprolol injection is given into a vein by a healthcare professional in a coronary care unit or similar setting, where your blood pressure, heart rate, and heart tracing can be watched. You are then switched to metoprolol tablets.

heading: Metoprolol dosage
text: The usual starting dose is 25 mg to 100 mg once a day for extended-release metoprolol, and 100 mg a day for immediate-release metoprolol. text: Q: Is it OK to drink alcohol with Prednisone? heading: What is rosuvastatin?
text: Rosuvastatin (Crestor) is a prescription medicine used to treat high cholesterol and to reduce the risk of major cardiovascular events such as heart attack and stroke. Rosuvastatin belongs to a class of medicines called statins. It works by blocking HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol. With cholesterol synthesis reduced, the liver increases its LDL receptors and clears more LDL, or "bad" cholesterol, from the blood. LDL and total cholesterol levels fall, with the maximum reduction usually reached by four weeks. Rosuvastatin comes as a tablet. It was first approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on August 12, 2003, under the brand name Crestor. Many generic versions of rosuvastatin tablets have since been approved.

heading: What is rosuvastatin used for?
text: Rosuvastatin is used: to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular (CV) events, such as death from cardiovascular disease, heart attack, stroke, or the need for procedures to improve blood flow to the heart called arterial revascularization, in adults at increased risk for these events. along with diet and exercise to lower the level of low-density lipoprotein (LDL-C) cholesterol or "bad" cholesterol: in adults with primary hypercholesterolemia. and slow the buildup of fatty deposits (plaque) in the walls of blood vessels in adults. in adults and children 8 years of age and older with high blood cholesterol due to heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH) (an inherited condition that causes high levels of LDL-C). in adults and children 7 years of age and older with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HoFH) (an inherited condition that causes high levels of LDL-C). along with diet for the treatment of adults with: primary dysbetalipoproteinemia (an inherited condition that causes high levels of cholesterol and fat). hypertriglyceridemia. It is not known if rosuvastatin is safe and effective in children younger than 8 years of age with HeFH, children younger than 7 years of age with HoFH, or in children with other types of hypercholesterolemia (other than HeFH or HoFH).

Your doctor may do blood tests to check your liver before you start taking this medicine and if you have symptoms of liver problems while you are taking it. heading: What is semaglutide?
text: Semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus) is a prescription GLP-1 medication used for weight loss and weight management, type 2 diabetes treatment, or to reduce the risk of chronic kidney disease and major cardiovascular events in certain patients with type 2 diabetes. Semaglutide (Wegovy) is also used to treat metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), without cirrhosis of the liver. Semaglutide injections are self-administered once weekly as an injection under the skin, and semaglutide pills are taken once daily. Semaglutide works by reducing appetite, delaying gastric emptying, increasing insulin release, and lowering the amount of glucagon released. Semaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist that mimics the behavior of the GLP-1 hormone, which is naturally released after eating. Semaglutide brand names are Ozempic, Rybelsus, and Wegovy, all made by Novo Nordisk. There is no generic semaglutide available. Semaglutide FDA approval was first granted on December 5, 2017, for the brand Ozempic. Each semaglutide brand or formulation is FDA-approved for specific conditions and patient populations.

heading: How does semaglutide work?
text: Semaglutide works by: Stimulates insulin production in the pancreas Reduces sugar production in the liver Slows down digestion, so food stays in the stomach longer Decreases appetite and food intake These combined actions help you feel full longer, eat less, and maintain better control over blood sugar levels. As a result, semaglutide supports weight loss, improves blood sugar management, and helps reduce the risk of cardiovascular events. Semaglutide's mechanism of action mimics a natural hormone in the body called GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1), which is released after eating to help regulate appetite and blood sugar levels. The way semaglutide works for kidney-related risk reduction is not fully understood. Semaglutide belongs to the drug class called GLP-1 receptor agonists.

They are not interchangeable, and the liquid gives a higher level of medicine in your blood for the same number of milligrams. You will need regular blood tests to check your potassium, sodium, kidney function, uric acid, and blood sugar. Keep these appointments even if you feel completely well. If you are being treated for high blood pressure, keep taking spironolactone even when you feel fine. High blood pressure usually has no symptoms. Tell any doctor or dentist treating you that you take spironolactone, and tell your surgeon before any operation. Spironolactone can interfere with one type of blood test used to measure digoxin, so mention it if you take digoxin. Do not share this medicine with anyone else. Store tablets at room temperature, 68°F to 77°F (20°C to 25°C), and protect them from light. Store the oral liquid at room temperature and keep it in a tightly closed bottle.

heading: What is the usual spironolactone dosage?
text: The usual starting dose of spironolactone tablets for adults is 25 mg to 100 mg a day, depending on the condition being treated. Your doctor will pick a starting dose and then adjust it based on your blood tests and how you respond. Spironolactone dosage for heart failure: Treatment starts at spironolactone 25 mg once a day, provided your potassium level is 5.0 mEq/L or lower and your kidney function (eGFR) is above 50. If you tolerate that, the dose may go up to 50 mg once a day. If your potassium rises too high, the dose may drop to 25 mg every other day. If your eGFR is between 30 and 50, your doctor may start you at 25 mg every other day because of the higher risk of high potassium. Spironolactone dosage for high blood pressure: The usual starting dose is spironolactone 25 mg to 100 mg a day, taken as one dose or split into two. The dose can be adjusted every two weeks. Doses above 100 mg a day do not generally lower blood pressure any further. Spironolactone dosage for fluid build-up (edema):

heading: What is the usual spironolactone dosage?
text: The usual starting dose is 100 mg a day, taken as one dose or split into two, and the dose can range from 25 mg to 200 mg a day. If you have cirrhosis, treatment is started in hospital and increased slowly. When spironolactone is the only water pill being used, it is given for at least five days before the dose is increased. Spironolactone dosage for primary hyperaldosteronism: The dose is 100 mg to 400 mg a day when preparing for surger y. For people who are not suitable for surgery, the lowest dose that works is used long term. Spironolactone oral liquid doses: The oral liquid has its own separate doses because it is absorbed differently. Heart failure starts at 20 mg (4 mL) once a day. High blood pressure starts at 20 mg (4 mL) to 75 mg (15 mL) a day. Swelling from cirrhosis starts at 75 mg (15 mL) a day, begun in hospital. If more than 100 mg a day is needed, a different form of the medicine should be used instead. Spironolactone formulations: Spironolactone 25 mg tablets Spironolactone 50 mg tablets Spironolactone 100 mg tablets Spironolactone oral suspension 25 mg per 5 mL

heading: What happens if I miss a dose?
text: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. Skip it if it is almost time for your next dose. Do not take two doses at once to make up for a missed one.

heading: What happens if I overdose?
text: Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. Taking too much spironolactone can cause drowsiness, confusion, a rash, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or diarrhea. A dangerously high potassium level is the main serious risk, particularly if your kidneys do not work well.

heading: What should I avoid while taking spironolactone?
text: Avoid potassium supplements, salt substitutes containing potassium, and low-sodium products that use potassium instead of salt. Check labels, since potassium chloride is a common salt replacement. Go easy on foods very high in potassium if your doctor has told you to. This is worth asking about specifically, because most people are told to eat more potassium, not less. Be careful with NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and naproxen. They can push your potassium up, make spironolactone work less well, and strain your kidneys. Limit alcohol. It can add to the dizziness and light-headedness, especially when you first start. Avoid getting up quickly from sitting or lying down, and avoid driving or anything hazardous until you know how spironolactone affects you. Do not take another medicine containing spironolactone at the same time, such as Aldactazide, and do not take eplerenone.

heading: What other drugs will affect spironolactone?
text: The most important interactions with spironolactone are medicines that also raise potassium, because the combined effect can push your level dangerously high. Tell your doctor about every medicine you take, including anything you start or stop during treatment. Be especially careful with: eplerenone, which should not be taken with spironolactone at all; medicines that raise potassium, including ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril and ramipril, ARBs such as losartan and valsartan, NSAIDs, heparin and low molecular weight heparin, and trimethoprim; potassium supplements and potassium-containing salt substitutes, which are usually stopped when spironolactone is started for heart failure; lithium, since spironolactone slows how fast your kidneys clear it and can cause lithium toxicity, so lithium levels need monitoring; digoxin, which needs care for two separate reasons: spironolactone interferes with one type of blood test used to measure digoxin, and it can also raise the actual amount of digoxin in your body; NSAIDs, which can also make spironolactone less effective as a water pill and as a blood pressure medicine; aspirin, which can reduce how well spironolactone works, so your dose may need adjusting; cholestyramine, which together with spironolactone has caused a high potassium level with too much acid in the blood; abiraterone, used in prostate cancer, which should not be combined with spironolactone because spironolactone attaches to the androgen receptor and can raise PSA readings; mitotane, which should be avoided because spironolactone lowers its level in the blood; and

heading: What other drugs will affect spironolactone?
text: other blood pressure medicines and water pills, which add to the blood pressure lowering effect. This list is not complete. Other prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products can interact with spironolactone. Give a list of all your medicines to any healthcare provider who treats you.

heading: Spironolactone FAQs
text: Is spironolactone a diuretic?: Yes. Spironolactone is a diuretic, or water pill, and it belongs to the group called potassium-sparing diuretics. It works by blocking aldosterone, a hormone that makes your kidneys hold onto salt and water. Unlike most water pills, which make you lose potassium, spironolactone makes your body keep potassium in. It is a weaker diuretic than medicines such as furosemide, which is one reason it is often given alongside another water pill rather than instead of one. Is spironolactone used for acne?: Spironolactone is not approved by the FDA for treating acne, but doctors sometimes prescribe it off-label for hormonal acne in women. Off-label means a doctor is prescribing a medicine for something other than its approved uses, which is legal and common, but it means the FDA has not reviewed the medicine for that purpose. The reason it is used this way relates to how spironolactone works. As well as blocking aldosterone, spironolactone attaches to the androgen receptor, the docking point for male hormones such as testosterone. Male hormones increase how much oil the skin produces, and oil production is one factor in acne. Because acne is not an approved use, there is no FDA-approved dose for it. Any dose is chosen by the prescriber. Spironolactone is generally avoided in pregnancy because it may affect how a male baby develops, which is an important consideration for anyone taking it for a skin condition rather than a heart or kidney condition.

heading: Spironolactone FAQs
text: If you are considering spironolactone for acne, this is a conversation to have with a doctor or dermatologist who can review your full medical history, since spironolactone still carries the same risk of raising your potassium level, whatever it is prescribed for. Does spironolactone cause weight gain?: Weight gain is not a recognized side effect of spironolactone, and it is not listed in the medicine's official prescribing information. Spironolactone is a diuretic, so it usually causes a small drop in weight in the first week or two as your body sheds extra fluid. If you are gaining weight while taking it, it is worth telling your doctor rather than assuming the medicine is to blame. Rapid weight gain with swelling in your ankles or legs or shortness of breath can be a sign of fluid building up, which may mean the condition being treated needs a closer look. Slower weight gain is more often down to appetite, activity, or another medicine. Does spironolactone cause hair loss?: Hair thinning, known as alopecia, is listed as a possible side effect of spironolactone, though how often it happens is not known. It is reported far less often than breast tenderness or breast growth.

heading: Spironolactone FAQs
text: The picture is complicated because spironolactone is also prescribed off label for hair loss in women, on the basis that blocking male hormones may help with hormone-related thinning. Spironolactone is not approved by the FDA for treating hair loss. If your hair is thinning while you take it, speak to your doctor, since there are several possible causes worth ruling out. How long does it take for spironolactone to work?: It depends what you are taking it for. Spironolactone reaches its highest level in your blood in about 2 to 3 hours, and its active breakdown product peaks at around 4 hours, so it starts having an effect on your kidneys the same day. The results you notice take longer. For fluid build-up, spironolactone is given for at least five days before the dose is increased, because that is how long the full effect takes to show. For high blood pressure, the dose is adjusted at two-week intervals, so give it a couple of weeks before judging it. For heart failure, the benefit is a lower risk of being admitted to hospital and living longer, which is not something you feel week to week. How long does spironolactone stay in your system?:

heading: Spironolactone FAQs
text: Spironolactone itself leaves your blood very quickly, with a half-life of about 1.4 hours, meaning half of it is gone in that time. Its active breakdown products last much longer, with half-lives of roughly 14 to 17 hours. Because of those, the effect of a dose carries on well after the spironolactone itself has gone, and it takes a few days for the medicine to clear fully after you stop. Clearance is slower if you have cirrhosis. Is spironolactone a blood thinner?: No. Spironolactone is not a blood thinner. It does not affect blood clotting and it is not used to prevent clots or strokes in the way that warfarin, apixaban, or aspirin are. It is a diuretic that lowers blood pressure and reduces fluid build-up. Spironolactone does interact with some blood thinners indirectly. Heparin and low molecular weight heparin can raise potassium, so taking them with spironolactone increases the risk of a high potassium level. Can I stop taking spironolactone suddenly?:

accepted.RefersTo: Heparin and low molecular weight heparin

heading: Spironolactone FAQs
text: Spironolactone does not cause withdrawal symptoms and does not need to be tapered the way a steroid does. Even so, do not stop it without speaking to your doctor. Stopping it can allow fluid to build up again, your blood pressure to rise, or your heart failure to worsen, and if you are taking it for heart failure it is one of the medicines shown to help people live longer. If side effects are the reason you want to stop, a dose change or a different medicine may be an option. Can you take spironolactone at night?: There is no fixed time of day for spironolactone. What matters more is that you take it at the same time each day and always the same way with regard to food, since food changes how much you absorb. Many people prefer the morning because spironolactone makes you pass more urine, and a late dose can mean getting up in the night. If a nighttime dose suits you better, check with your doctor or pharmacist first. Can you drink alcohol while taking spironolactone?: There is no direct interaction between alcohol and spironolactone, but drinking is best kept modest. Both can lower your blood pressure and make you light-headed, so together they raise the chance of feeling dizzy or faint, particularly when you stand up. Alcohol is also a problem in its own right if you are taking spironolactone for liver disease. Ask your doctor what is reasonable for your situation.

heading: Spironolactone FAQs
text: Can you take spironolactone while pregnant?: Spironolactone is generally avoided in pregnancy. It blocks the action of male hormones, and in animal studies male offspring exposed before birth developed abnormally. Human data are limited and have not shown a clear increase in birth defects, but the concern is enough that the manufacturer advises avoiding it or discussing the potential risk to a male baby. Do not stop spironolactone on your own if you find out you are pregnant. Tell your doctor straight away, because untreated heart failure, cirrhosis, and high blood pressure also carry serious risks in pregnancy and your treatment will need to be changed carefully. Does spironolactone cause constipation?: Constipation is not a listed side effect of spironolactone. The digestive side effects that have been reported are the opposite, including diarrhea and stomach cramping, along with nausea, vomiting, and indigestion. If you are constipated while taking spironolactone, another cause is more likely, and it is worth mentioning to your pharmacist, who can check the rest of your medicines. Is 200 mg of spironolactone too much?: It depends on the reason you are taking it. For fluid build-up, the approved dose range goes up to 200 mg a day, and for primary hyperaldosteronism it goes up to 400 mg a day, so 200 mg is within the licensed range for both.

heading: Spironolactone FAQs
text: For high blood pressure it would be above the usual range, since doses over 100 mg a day do not lower blood pressure any further. For heart failure the usual dose is 25 mg to 50 mg a day, so 200 mg would be well above what is normally used. Higher doses also carry a greater risk of high potassium and of breast growth in men. If your dose seems high for your condition, ask your prescriber rather than adjusting it yourself. Why is spironolactone described as a high-risk medicine?: The main reason is the risk of a high potassium level, which can cause a dangerous change in your heart rhythm and often gives no warning symptoms. The risk rises if your kidneys do not work well or if you take other medicines that raise potassium, and several very common medicines do, including ibuprofen and some blood pressure tablets. This risk is manageable, which is why blood tests are built into treatment. Your potassium should be checked within a week of starting spironolactone or changing your dose, and regularly after that. Spironolactone also needs care in pregnancy and in people with liver disease.

heading: Popular FAQ
text: Q: Winlevi vs Spironolactone: How do they compare? A: Winlevi (clascoterone) and spironolactone are both prescribed to treat acne. Winlevi is a topical cream, while spironolactone is available in an oral tablet and oral suspension.

heading: What is tamsulosin?
text: Tamsulosin is used to treat the symptoms of an enlarged prostate, also called benign prostatic hyperplasia or BPH. These symptoms include a weak urine stream, trouble starting to urinate, dribbling, a feeling of not emptying the bladder completely, needing to urinate often or urgently, and getting up at night to urinate. Tamsulosin belongs to a group of medicines called alpha blockers. It works by blocking alpha-1 receptors in the prostate and bladder neck. Blocking these receptors relaxes the muscle there, which improves urine flow and eases BPH symptoms. Tamsulosin is taken once daily, about half an hour after the same meal each day. Capsules should be swallowed whole and not crushed, chewed, or opened. The tamsulosin brand name was Flomax, which has now been discontinued in the U.S., but generic tamsulosin is available. Tamsulosin is not approved to treat high blood pressure, and it is not approved for use in women or children.

heading: Warnings and precautions
text: Do not take tamsulosin if you are allergic to tamsulosin or to any of the ingredients in the capsule. Do not take tamsulosin with other alpha blockers such as alfuzosin (Uroxatral), doxazosin (Cardura), prazosin (Minipress), silodosin (Rapaflo), or terazosin (Hytrin). Do not take tamsulosin 0.4 mg with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor such as ketoconazole. These medicines raise tamsulosin levels in your blood. Tamsulosin can lower your blood pressure when you stand up, which may make you feel dizzy or faint. This is most likely when you first start taking it, when your dose changes, or when you start it again after a break. Get up slowly from sitting or lying down. Be careful driving or doing anything that needs you to be alert until you know how tamsulosin affects you. In rare cases (probably fewer than 1 in 50,000 patients), tamsulosin can cause priapism, a painful erection that lasts a long time and is not related to sexual activity. Get medical help straight away if this happens, because without prompt treatment it can lead to permanent erectile dysfunction. An enlarged prostate and prostate cancer can occur together. Ask your doctor about prostate cancer screening before you start tamsulosin and at regular intervals while you are taking it.

heading: Warnings and precautions
text: Tamsulosin can cause a problem called intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS) during cataract or glaucoma surgery. Tell your eye surgeon that you take tamsulosin or have taken it in the past, even if you stopped months ago. Do not stop taking tamsulosin before surgery unless your surgeon tells you to. If you are already booked in for cataract or glaucoma surgery, starting tamsulosin is not recommended. If you stop taking tamsulosin for several days, talk to your doctor before starting again. You will need to restart at the 0.4 mg dose. Many other medicines can interact with tamsulosin. Tell your doctor about everything you take, including prescription medicines, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.

heading: Before taking this medicine
text: To make sure tamsulosin is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had: an allergy to tamsulosin or any of its ingredients an allergy to sulfa drugs kidney problems liver problems low blood pressure (hypotension) Also tell your doctor if you are planning to have cataract or glaucoma surgery. Ask your doctor about prostate cancer screening before starting tamsulosin and at regular intervals afterwards. Tamsulosin is not approved for use in women or in children.

heading: How should I take tamsulosin?
text: Take tamsulosin exactly as prescribed. Follow the directions on your prescription label and read any medication guides or instruction sheets. Take once a day, about 30 minutes after the same meal each day. For example, 30 minutes after dinner. Swallow the capsule whole. Do not crush, chew, break, or open it. If you stop taking tamsulosin for several days, do not start again without talking to your doctor. Store at room temperature, away from moisture and heat. Dosing information: Usual adult dose for benign prostatic hyperplasia: 0.4 mg by mouth once a day, taken about half an hour after the same meal each day. If symptoms have not improved after 2 to 4 weeks at 0.4 mg, the dose may be increased to 0.8 mg once a day. Tamsulosin 0.4 mg should not be taken with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor such as ketoconazole. If tamsulosin is stopped or interrupted for several days, treatment should start again at 0.4 mg once a day.

heading: What happens if I miss a dose?
text: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If you have missed the dose for the whole day, skip it and take your next dose at the usual time. Do not take two doses at once. If you stop taking tamsulosin for several days in a row, talk to your doctor before starting again.

heading: What happens if I overdose?
text: Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. An overdose can cause a serious drop in blood pressure. Lying down flat can help until medical help arrives.

heading: What should I avoid while taking tamsulosin?
text: Avoid driving or other activities that could be dangerous until you know how tamsulosin affects you. It can make you feel dizzy or lightheaded. Avoid getting up too quickly from sitting or lying down, or you may feel dizzy.

heading: Tamsulosin side effects
text: Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction, such as hives, itching, rash, swelling of your face, tongue, or throat, or trouble breathing. Rarely, tamsulosin has been linked to severe skin reactions with blistering and peeling of the skin. Stop taking tamsulosin and call your doctor at once if you have: a lightheaded feeling, like you might pass out a painful erection that will not go away and is not related to sexual activity What are the common side effects of tamsulosin?: Common tamsulosin side effects may include: headache dizziness runny or stuffy nose, sore throat, cough, sinus congestion flu-like symptoms or infection weakness or lack of energy back pain, chest pain diarrhea, nausea drowsiness or trouble sleeping tooth problems abnormal ejaculation, including a smaller amount of semen or no semen at all reduced interest in sex blurred vision Some side effects are more likely at the higher 0.8 mg dose than at the usual 0.4 mg starting dose. In clinical studies, abnormal ejaculation was reported by about 8 in 100 men taking 0.4 mg and about 18 in 100 men taking 0.8 mg. Blurred vision was reported by about 2 in 100 men taking 0.8 mg, and was uncommon at 0.4 mg. This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

heading: What other drugs will affect tamsulosin?
text: Tamsulosin is broken down in the body mainly by two liver enzymes, CYP3A4 and CYP2D6. Medicines that block these enzymes can raise the amount of tamsulosin in your blood and increase the risk of side effects. Do not take tamsulosin with: strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as ketoconazole other alpha blockers, such as alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin, silodosin, or terazosin Use with caution, and tell your doctor if you take: moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as erythromycin strong CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as paroxetine, or moderate CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as terbinafine cimetidine warfarin medicines for erectile dysfunction or pulmonary arterial hypertension known as PDE5 inhibitors, including avanafil (Stendra), sildenafil (Viagra, Revatio), tadalafil (Adcirca, Cialis), and vardenafil (Levitra). Taking these with tamsulosin can lower blood pressure enough to cause symptoms. Some of these cautions matter more at the higher 0.8 mg dose than at 0.4 mg. Your doctor will decide what is right for you. No dose change is needed if you take tamsulosin with nifedipine, atenolol, enalapril, digoxin, theophylline, or furosemide. This list is not complete, and many other medicines may interact with tamsulosin. This includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.
