heading: What is Tirzepatide?
text: Tirzepatide is a once-weekly injection available as two brands: Zepbound (for weight loss, weight management, and obstructive sleep apnea) and Mounjaro (for type 2 diabetes and to lower the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in those with type 2 diabetes at high risk). Zepbound (tirzepatide) is FDA-approved for weight loss and weight management in adults with obesity, or in overweight adults with at least one weight-related medical condition. Zepbound is also approved to treat moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in adults with obesity. Mounjaro (tirzepatide) is FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes in adults and children aged 10 years and older to help improve blood sugar (glucose) levels, used alongside diet and exercise. It is also approved to lower the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack, or non-fatal stroke) in adults with type 2 diabetes who are at high risk for these events. Tirzepatide is a dual GIP/ GLP-1 receptor agonist, meaning it activates two gut hormone receptors that help regulate appetite, digestion, and blood sugar. It works by reducing appetite, increasing feelings of fullness, slowing gastric emptying, boosting insulin release when blood sugar is high, and reducing glucagon secretion. Tirzepatide is self-administered as a subcutaneous (under the skin) injection using a single-dose pen, KwikPen, or vial with syringe, and should always be used together with diet and exercise. Tirzepatide should not be used in people with type 1 diabetes. It is not known if tirzepatide is safe in people who have had pancreatitis.

heading: How Much Weight Can You Lose on Tirzepatide?
text: Patients on Tirzepatide 15 mg weekly lost an average of 20.9% or 48.6 lb of their body weight after 72 weeks in the Zepbound Study 1 (NCT04184622) compared to placebo patients who lost an average of 3.1% or 7.2 lb. Study 1 was a 72-week trial comparing Zepbound weight loss with placebo in adults with obesity or overweight with at least one weight-related condition, excluding patients with type 2 diabetes. Zepbound Weight Loss Results at 72 Weeks by Dose: Treatment dose | Average % weight loss | Average weight lost | Average starting weight Zepbound 5 mg | 15.0% | 34.0 lb | 226.9 lb Zepbound 10 mg | 19.5% | 45.5 lb | 233.2 lb Zepbound 15 mg | 20.9% | 48.6 lb | 232.8 lb Placebo | 3.1% | 7.2 lb | 231.0 lb

heading: Mounjaro HbA1c Results for Type 2 Diabetes
text: In the Mounjaro prescribing information, SURPASS-1 (NCT03954834) was a 40-week trial in adults with type 2 diabetes whose blood sugar was not adequately controlled with diet and exercise alone. Patients received once-weekly Mounjaro 5 mg, 10 mg, or 15 mg, or placebo. After 40 weeks, 78% to 85% of adults taking Mounjaro achieved an HbA1c below 7%, compared with 23% of adults taking a placebo. The average HbA1c change was -1.8% with Mounjaro 5 mg, -1.7% with Mounjaro 10 mg, and -1.7% with Mounjaro 15 mg, compared with -0.1% with placebo.

heading: Mounjaro Results for Reducing Cardiovascular Risk
text: SURPASS-CVOT randomized 13,299 adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease to Mounjaro (tirzepatide, up to 15 mg once weekly) or dulaglutide 1.5 mg once weekly, a GLP-1 medicine already approved to reduce cardiovascular risk, with a median follow-up of about 4 years. Cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack, or non-fatal stroke occurred in 12.1% of those taking Mounjaro compared with 13.0% of those taking dulaglutide (HR 0.92, 95.3% CI 0.83–1.01), meeting the trial's goal of non-inferiority but not demonstrating superiority. Death from any cause occurred in 8.5% of the Mounjaro group versus 10.1% of the dulaglutide group (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.75–0.94), though this was not a primary endpoint and was not adjusted for multiple comparisons, so it should be read as exploratory. Because the comparator was an active medicine rather than placebo, these results describe how Mounjaro performs against another GLP-1, not how much it lowers risk compared with no treatment.

heading: Tirzepatide side effects
text: Common Side Effects: The most common tirzepatide side effects are: Diarrhea Vomiting Constipation Nausea (mild to moderate) Decreased appetite Abdominal pain. Serious side effects: Tirzepatide can cause serious side effects. Call your doctor right away if you have any of the following: Severe stomach pain (pancreatitis): Stop taking tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider immediately if you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away, with or without vomiting, or pain that spreads to your back. Kidney problems: Diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting can cause dehydration, which may lead to kidney problems. Drink plenty of fluids to reduce this risk and tell your doctor if you are unable to keep fluids down. Gallbladder problems: Symptoms include severe upper stomach pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), or clay-colored stools. Serious allergic reactions: Seek emergency medical attention if you experience hives, difficulty breathing, feeling light-headed, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat (anaphylaxis or angioedema). Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia): Symptoms may include headache, hunger, weakness, sweating, confusion, irritability, dizziness, fast heart rate, or feeling jittery. Vision changes: Tell your doctor about any blurred vision or other vision changes, particularly if you have type 2 diabetes. Thyroid tumor: Symptoms may include a lump or swelling in your neck, trouble swallowing, hoarseness, or shortness of breath. Mental health changes: Tell your healthcare provider right away about any new or worsening depression, mood changes, or thoughts of suicide or self-harm.

heading: Tirzepatide side effects
text: Aspiration during surgery: Tirzepatide slows stomach emptying, which may increase the risk of food or liquid entering the lungs during procedures using anesthesia or sedation. Tell all your healthcare providers you are taking tirzepatide before any planned surgery or procedure. This is not a complete list of side effects. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects, or report them to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

heading: Important Safety Information
text: Who should not use tirzepatide: Type 1 diabetes patients (tirzepatide is not approved for type 1 diabetes) Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2). Use with Caution: History of pancreatitis (safety not established in patients with prior pancreatitis) Severe gastrointestinal disease Diabetic retinopathy complications.

heading: Warnings
text: Tirzepatide carries a Boxed Warning for the risk of possible thyroid tumors. Possible Thyroid Tumors (Including Cancer): Tell your healthcare provider if you get a lump or swelling in your neck, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, or shortness of breath. These may be symptoms of thyroid cancer. In studies with rats, tirzepatide and medicines that work like tirzepatide have caused thyroid tumors, including thyroid cancer. It is not known if tirzepatide will cause thyroid tumors, or a type of thyroid cancer called medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) in people. Do not use tirzepatide if you or any of your family have ever had a type of thyroid cancer called medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), or if you have an endocrine system condition called Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).

heading: Before using tirzepatide
text: Tell your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to tirzepatide, any other medications, or any of the ingredients in this medicine. There is a list of ingredients in this medicine, at the bottom of this page. Tell your healthcare team if you are planning surgery or other procedure that uses anesthesia or deep sedation. Tell your doctor if you have or have ever had kidney or pancreas disease, a history of diabetic retinopathy or any stomach problems such as difficulty digesting food. Tell your doctor if you plan to become pregnant, are pregnant, or are breastfeeding. If you become pregnant while taking this medicine, you should tell your doctor. There is a pregnancy exposure registry for women who take Zepbound during pregnancy. Talk to your healthcare provider about how you can take part, call 1-844-524-0039, or visit https://pregnancyregistry.lilly.com/zepbound.

heading: What is the cost of tirzepatide?
text: The cost of tirzepatide depends on your insurance plan, pharmacy, and the brand you use. Zepbound cost Zepbound may cost $25 for a 1-month or 3-month pen prescription if you have commercial insurance and are eligible for the Savings Card. Note that patients with government insurance (Medicare, Medicaid) are not eligible for the savings card. heading: How should I use tirzepatide?
text: You should follow the directions on your prescription label carefully and ask your pharmacist or doctor to explain any part you do not understand. It is important to use this medicine exactly as directed. Do not take more or less of it or take it more often than prescribed by your doctor. Tirzepatide is injected under the skin (subcutaneously) using a pre-filled single-dose pen, a multi-dose KwikPen (for single patient use), and a single-dose vial with a syringe. Caregivers or patients should be trained on proper injection techniques and should read the instructions for use. Children should not inject themselves with the KwikPen; an adult caregiver should give a child their injections. Tirzepatide is usually given: once a week. can be given with or without meals at any time of the day. may be injected into the thigh, abdomen, or have another person inject it into the back of your upper arm You should rotate injection sites with each dose. Do not inject into a muscle (intramuscularly) or vein (intravenously). Do not mix insulin and tirzepatide together in the same injection. You may give an injection of tirzepatide and insulin in the same body area, but not right next to each other. Your doctor will probably start you on a low dose, which may be gradually increased, but not more than once every 4 weeks. You may change the day of the week you use tirzepatide as long as there are at least three days between doses.

heading: How should I use tirzepatide?
text: Do not stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor. Tirzepatide KwikPen: The KwikPen contains 4 fixed doses, and one dose is injected weekly (subcutaneously). The Pen will prevent you from dialing a full dose after you have given yourself 4 weekly doses. Do not inject the leftover medicine. Do not transfer the leftover medicine from your Pen into a syringe. Do not share your tirzepatide Pen with other people, even if the pen needle has been changed. heading: Dosing Information
text: Usual Zepbound Dose for Weight Loss and OSA (Adult): Initial dose: 2.5 mg under the skin (subcutaneously) once a week. After 4 weeks: The dosage should be increased to 5 mg subcutaneously once a week. Further dose increases: After at least 4 weeks on the current dose, the dosage may be increased in 2.5 mg increments. Recommended maintenance dose for weight loss: 5 mg, 10 mg, or 15 mg injected subcutaneously once weekly. Recommended maintenance dose for OSA: 10 mg or 15 mg injected subcutaneously once weekly. Maximum dose: 15 mg subcutaneously once a week. Dose of Mounjaro for Type 2 Diabetes (Adults and Children 10 Years and Older): Initial dose: 2.5 mg subcutaneously once a week. If additional glycemic control is needed: Increase the dose in 2.5 mg increments after at least 4 weeks on the current dose. Maximum dose (adults): 15 mg subcutaneously once a week. Dose of Mounjaro to Reduce Cardiovascular Risk (Adults With Type 2 Diabetes at High Risk): The same dosing and escalation schedule applies. Start at 2.5 mg subcutaneously once a week and increase in 2.5 mg increments after at least 4 weeks on the current dose, up to a maximum of 15 mg once a week. In the SURPASS-CVOT trial, participants were titrated to 15 mg once weekly or their maximum tolerated dose.

heading: Dosing Information
text: How to Use Mounjaro: Give once weekly at any time of day, with or without meals. Inject subcutaneously into the abdomen or thigh. Another person may inject into the back of the upper arm. Rotate injection sites with each dose. Missed dose: Give as soon as possible within 4 days (96 hours). If more than 4 days have passed, skip the missed dose and give the next dose on the regularly scheduled day. The day of weekly administration can be changed, if necessary, as long as the time between the 2 doses is at least 3 days (72 hours).

heading: What should I do if I miss a dose?
text: If you miss a dose of tirzepatide, take the missed dose as soon as you remember it, if within 4 days after the missed dose. However, if it has been more than 4 days since your last dose, then skip the missed dose and continue your regular dosing schedule. Do not inject two doses within 3 days of each other.

heading: What happens if I overdose?
text: In case of overdose, call the poison control helpline at 1-800-222-1222. Information is also available online at Poison Help. If the victim has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing, or can't be awakened, immediately call emergency services at 911.

heading: Do you regain weight after stopping tirzepatide?

heading: Popular FAQ
text: Q: Zepbound vs Mounjaro: Comparison Guide for Weight Loss and Diabetes Treatment A: Zepbound and Mounjaro contain tirzepatide and are made by Eli Lilly. They are both administered as a once-weekly subcutaneous injection, but they have different FDA-approved indications and insurance coverage. Q: Which GLP-1 drug is best for weight loss? A: The most effective GLP-1 drug for weight loss currently (as of early 2026) is tirzepatide, marketed under the names Zepbound (for weight loss) and Mounjaro (for diabetes). Clinical trials and recent meta-analyses consistently show tirzepatide delivers the most substantial weight reduction among GLP-1 medications, with average losses of up to 22.5% of body weight. Q: How long does it take for Mounjaro (tirzepatide) to start working? A: Mounjaro (generic name: tirzepatide) will start to lower your blood sugar levels right away but it can take 8 to 12 weeks to reach your target A1C goal. When compared to some other diabetes treatments, studies have shown that it can take 8 weeks to reach an A1C target of ≤7% and 12 weeks to reach an A1C ≤6.5% with Mounjaro. Significant weight loss can occur as early as 28-weeks. Q: Tirzepatide vs semaglutide: How do they compare? A: Semaglutide and tirzepatide are prescription medicines used for type 2 diabetes and long-term weight management. Semaglutide products include Ozempic, Rybelsus, Wegovy, and Wegovy HD, while tirzepatide products include Mounjaro and Zepbound. These medicines differ in dosing, approved uses, side effects, and cost, so discuss options with your healthcare provider.

heading: What is tramadol?
text: Tramadol is an opioid agonist that may be used to treat moderate to moderately severe chronic pain in adults, when other pain treatments such as non-opioid pain medicines do not treat your pain well enough, or you cannot tolerate them. Extended-release forms of tramadol may be used in adults who require around-the-clock treatment of their pain for an extended period. An opioid pain medicine such as tramadol can put you at risk for overdose and death. Even if you take your dose correctly as prescribed, you are at risk for opioid addiction, abuse, and misuse that can lead to death. Brands of tramadol include ConZip, Qdolo, Ryzolt, Ultram, Ultram ER, and Ultracet. Many have been discontinued, but generic tramadol is still available. Taking tramadol in combination with other pain-relieving medicines such as acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or aspirin can provide better pain relief than just taking one pain-relieving medicine by itself (see Can you take tramadol in combination with acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or aspirin?) Tramadol first gained FDA approval on March 3, 1995. Originally, it was classified as a non-controlled substance, but it was reclassified in 2014 to Schedule IV of the Controlled Substances Act with restrictions on its prescribing. Tramadol is an opioid (see Is tramadol an opioid?). A person's genetics can affect the pain-relieving properties of tramadol (see How do genetics affect tramadol?).

heading: Tramadol uses
text: Tramadol is used for the management of moderate to moderately severe pain in adults, including postoperative pain (pain after surgery). Tramadol treats pain severe enough to require opioids and may be used as an alternative to other forms of pain relief that did not relieve pain well enough or were not tolerated. Tramadol extended-release capsules may be used by adults who require around-the-clock treatment of their moderate to moderately severe chronic pain for an extended time. Tramadol should not be used in children younger than 12 years old, or anyone younger than 18 years old with other risk factors (such as breathing problems), or who have recently had surgery to remove their tonsils or adenoids. Extended-release tramadol (Ultram ER) should not be given to anyone younger than 18 years.

heading: Is Tramadol an opioid?
text: Yes, tramadol is an opioid. The opioid activity of tramadol is due to its binding to mu-opioid receptors.

heading: Important Information About Tramadol
text: Get emergency help or call 911 right away if you take too many tramadol (overdose). When you first start taking tramadol, when your dose is changed, or if you take too much (overdose), serious or life-threatening breathing problems that can lead to death may occur. Ask your healthcare provider about medicines like naloxone or nalmefene that can be used in an emergency to reverse an opioid overdose. Taking tramadol with other opioid medicines, benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids (gabapentin or pregabalin), alcohol, or other central nervous system depressants (including street drugs) can cause severe drowsiness, decreased awareness, breathing problems, coma, and death. Do not take tramadol with any other medicine that contains tramadol. Check the label of every pain medicine you take, as some combination products contain tramadol. You should be given a Medication Guide each time you fill a tramadol prescription. Read it every time, even if you have taken tramadol before, because the information may have changed. Your healthcare provider or pharmacist should also go through the risks of tramadol and how to take it safely with you, and explain what to do in an emergency. Never give anyone else your tramadol. They could die from taking it. Selling or giving away tramadol is against the law. Store tramadol securely, out of sight and reach of children, and in a location not accessible by others, including visitors to the home.

heading: Tramadol side effects
text: Common side effects: The most common side effects of tramadol are: dizziness or vertigo nausea constipation headache drowsiness vomiting itching. Dry mouth is also commonly reported with the extended-release forms of tramadol. A person's genetics can affect their response to tramadol, including their risk of side effects (see How do genetics affect tramadol?). Serious tramadol side effects and warnings: Tramadol may cause serious side effects, some of which may be fatal. Tramadol can slow or stop your breathing and may be habit-forming. MISUSE OF THIS MEDICINE CAN CAUSE ADDICTION, OVERDOSE, OR DEATH, especially in a child or other person using the medicine without a prescription. Keep this medicine where others cannot get to it. Do not take more tramadol than prescribed, as an overdose can be fatal. Selling or giving away this medicine is against the law. A person caring for you should give naloxone and seek emergency medical attention if you have slow breathing with long pauses, blue-colored lips, or if you find it hard to wake up. Serious breathing problems may be more likely in older adults and people who are debilitated or have wasting syndrome or chronic breathing disorders.

heading: Tramadol side effects
text: Call your doctor at once if you have: noisy breathing, sighing, shallow breathing, breathing that stops during sleep a slow heart rate or weak pulse a light-headed feeling, like you might pass out seizure (convulsions) or low cortisol levels (symptoms include nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, dizziness, worsening tiredness or weakness) low sodium levels (hyponatremia). Symptoms include headache, confusion, weakness, unsteadiness, or feeling sick low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Symptoms include shakiness, sweating, hunger, confusion, or a fast heartbeat. Seek medical attention right away if you have symptoms of serotonin syndrome, such as agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness, twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Seizures have been reported in patients taking tramadol. Your risk of seizures is higher if you are taking higher doses than recommended. Seizure risk is also higher in those with epilepsy or a history of seizures, and in those taking certain antidepressants, other opioids, MAO inhibitors, or other medicines that lower the seizure threshold. You should not take tramadol if you have significant breathing problems, acute or severe asthma in a setting where you cannot be monitored, a blockage in your stomach or intestines, or if you have taken an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days (isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, tranylcypromine, and others). Tell your doctor before starting tramadol if you have a head injury or increased pressure inside your skull, as tramadol should be used with particular care in these situations.

heading: Tramadol side effects
text: Prescribers are advised not to prescribe tramadol for people who are suicidal or prone to addiction, and to use it with caution in people taking tranquilizers or antidepressants, or drinking heavily. If you are struggling with thoughts of harming yourself, or with your use of any medicine, tell your healthcare provider so they can help you find the right treatment and support. Fatal side effects can occur if you use this medicine with alcohol, or with other drugs that cause drowsiness or slow your breathing. People taking extended-release forms of tramadol should not consume alcohol-containing beverages at the same time. Alcohol is also not advised with immediate-release forms of tramadol. Serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, have occurred with tramadol, some of which caused death. People who are allergic to other opioids are at higher risk. Other hypersensitivity reactions include itching, hives, narrowing of the airways, swelling of the face and airways (angioedema), and serious skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson Syndrome. Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to tramadol (symptoms include hives, difficulty breathing, swelling in your face or throat) or a severe skin reaction (fever, sore throat, burning in your eyes, skin pain, a red or purple skin rash that spreads and causes blistering and peeling).

heading: Tramadol side effects
text: Tramadol may make pain worse rather than better in some people, an effect called opioid-induced hyperalgesia. Talk to your doctor if the pain you have increases, if you feel more sensitive to pain, or if you have new pain after taking tramadol. Tramadol extended-release capsules and tablets may complicate a healthcare provider’s clinical assessment of an acute abdominal condition. They are not recommended for people with severe liver or severe kidney impairment. Taking tramadol during pregnancy may cause life-threatening withdrawal symptoms in the newborn, known as neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS). Some people are “ultra-rapid metabolizers” of tramadol because of a variation in an enzyme called CYP2D6. Their bodies convert tramadol into its active form faster than usual, which can produce dangerously high opioid levels even at a normal dose. Life-threatening breathing problems and deaths have occurred in children for this reason, including after surgery to remove the tonsils or adenoids. Tramadol should not be given to a child younger than 12 years old, or to anyone younger than 18 years old who has recently had surgery to remove the tonsils or adenoids. Extended-release tramadol should not be given to anyone younger than 18 years. Tramadol may cause drowsiness or affect your ability to drive or perform hazardous tasks. Do not perform these tasks if tramadol causes confusion, mental impairment, or drowsiness.

heading: Tramadol side effects
text: Tramadol can cause withdrawal symptom s if stopped suddenly after being taken for a long period of time. Symptoms may include restlessness, drug craving, anxiety, and sweating. Do not stop taking tramadol suddenly without talking to your healthcare provider, as stopping abruptly can cause serious withdrawal symptoms and uncontrolled pain (see How long does tramadol withdrawal last?). This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Seizures have occurred in some people taking tramadol. Your seizure risk may be higher if you have ever had: a head injury, epilepsy, or other seizure disorder drug or alcohol addiction or a metabolic disorder. heading: Before taking this medicine
text: Tramadol may harm an unborn baby and is not usually recommended during pregnancy. Use of tramadol for an extended period of time during pregnancy can cause withdrawal symptoms in your newborn baby that could be life-threatening if not recognized and treated. Neonatal seizures, neonatal withdrawal syndrome, fetal death, and stillbirth have all been reported. Tramadol is also not recommended during or immediately before labor. It should only be used in pregnancy if the benefits outweigh the risks. If you are already taking tramadol and become pregnant, do not stop taking it without talking to your healthcare provider, as stopping suddenly can be harmful to you both. Breastfeeding: Breastfeeding is not recommended while taking tramadol, as it may harm your baby. Mothers who are ultra-rapid metabolizers of tramadol can have higher than expected levels of its active form in their breast milk, which can be dangerous for a breastfed infant. Carefully observe infants for increased sleepiness (more than usual), breathing difficulties, or limpness. Seek immediate medical care if you notice these signs.

heading: How should I take tramadol?
text: Do not change your dose. Take tramadol exactly as prescribed by your healthcare provider. Use the lowest dose possible for the shortest time needed. Tell your doctor if you feel an increased urge to take more of this medicine. For acute (short-term) pain, you may only need to take tramadol for a few days. You may have some tramadol left over that you did not use. See disposal information at the bottom of this section for directions on how to safely dispose of tramadol. Take your prescribed dose as indicated by your healthcare provider. Take your prescribed dose as indicated by your healthcare provider. After your dose has been settled, immediate-release tramadol is usually taken as 50 mg to 100 mg (one or two 50 mg tablets) every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain. Do not take more than your prescribed dose, and do not take more than 400 mg of tramadol in one day. For immediate-release tramadol, that is eight 50 mg tablets a day, taken in divided doses, or 80 mL of the 5 mg/mL oral solution. Extended-release tramadol has a lower daily limit of 300 mg, taken as one dose once a day. Always check the strength printed on your own bottle or packet. Do not take tramadol together with any other medicine that contains tramadol. If you miss a dose, take your next dose at your usual time.

heading: How should I take tramadol?

heading: Popular FAQ
text: Q: How long do venlafaxine withdrawal symptoms last? A: Venlafaxine withdrawal symptoms typically last up to 1 to 4 weeks, but may persist even longer. The timing varies widely. People who stop suddenly, took higher doses, or used venlafaxine for years may have symptoms for two to three months or longer. Q: What drugs can cause serotonin syndrome? A: Common drug classes that can cause serotonin syndrome include selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs), and opioids like tramadol.
